sections.heading: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Every workflow starts in SAM with hard filters. Kizzy Parks's 2026 search goes to Search, then Contracting, and selects Solicitation plus Combined Solicitation, due next month, with a total small business set-aside. That search returned 1,683 live results, and Parks steers beginners toward non-controversial 'entrepreneurial' work [qVThWm83wus @ 00:03:09]. James Walk scans every solicitation opened in the last 24 hours, about 1,000 a day this quarter, and filters for VA and fitness. Walk keeps 12 federal tabs, 5 Texas tabs and 1 MAS tab open at once [AHQVro9N9HM @ 00:02:30]. Dr. Wes Fisher's five-day plan spends day one searching Contract Opportunities with both active and inactive boxes checked, which shows 5.1M results. From there the operator lists 15 to 20 opportunities and works only one to three of them [xH6KWT7x8Ac @ 00:02:17]. Ricky Howard targets earlier signals: a sources sought, RFI or acquisition forecast that matches 50 to 80 percent of what you do. Howard then sends the office clarifying questions, so you are already in communication with the buyer before you call any teaming partner [z6ZNrmprd-o @ 00:03:02]. The four methods differ in detail, but each runs the same daily discipline. Scan wide, filter narrow, and commit to only a handful of targets you can quote quickly.

Once a target is picked, the work happens on the phone. Fisher's script asks subs exactly two things: 'can you do the job how much you're going to cost that's it.' Fisher holds that 'there's no reason why you shouldn't be able to get a quote in 48 hours.' Days two and three are for calls, and day four is for watching the inbox [xH6KWT7x8Ac @ 00:02:55]. Parks wants three to five quotes, preferably local, but warns against assuming geography, since a New Mexico firm may serve nationally [kpISY6VCkNY @ 00:01:39]. James Walk's VA Dallas cooling-tower win shows what that digging buys. Only one Texas distributor carried the parts, and the distributor said Walk was the fifth caller. Walk proposed two to three weeks against a 100-day requirement and attached the distributor's 'authorized customer' letter. Walk also caught part-number errors (O versus 0) and delivered in under ten days [AHQVro9N9HM @ 00:04:48]. For teaming, Howard contacts about five firms with past performance at the target agency. The pitch is that you are already talking with the office and can do part of the work while they do the rest. Howard expects three of five to say yes, finds that calling beats email, and never sends the link or exact opportunity, only generalities [z6ZNrmprd-o @ 00:04:59].

The pricing numbers cluster tightly. A contracting officer told Parks that newcomers bid too low or too high. The middle is 7 to 25 percent, and on gravel the sweet spot was 10 to 13 percent [etvo2gL7_Cs @ 00:02:23]. Walk won the cooling-tower job at a 15 percent markup on about $42K of parts, for 'three phone calls and 10 emails,' and was not the lowest bidder [AHQVro9N9HM @ 00:08:02]. Robert Harvey III's incumbent rule: if the incumbent charged $2, bid around $2.25, not $7 or $8 [YHptbPFEaPQ @ 00:08:20]. A contracting officer also told Harvey to add 5 to 10 percent per year for inflation on five-year contracts [YHptbPFEaPQ @ 00:07:27]. Parks's Tammy's Toilets math shows how margin stacks down the chain. The prime is paid $100, pays Tammy $50 and keeps 50 percent. Tammy spends $5 on equipment and $10 on labor and keeps $35, and the cleaners keep $5 of their $10 [kpISY6VCkNY @ 00:04:14]. Invoice monthly and expect payment in 15 to 30 days typically, or 30 to 60 on average. Speed it up by emailing your POC with the invoice attached [kpISY6VCkNY @ 00:03:16]. Walk matched terms on both ends, with the distributor on net 30 and the government on net 30, and only bid what Walk could cover [AHQVro9N9HM @ 00:11:31].

sop_steps.title: Build the Target List
sop_steps.action: Spend day one listing 15-20 SAM opportunities, then narrow to the 1-3 you will actually work.
sop_steps.detail: Fisher's day-one rule is 'shoot for like 15 or 20 on your list' and then work one to three of them [Dr. Wes Fisher — xH6KWT7x8Ac @ 00:02:17]. Walk feeds the same list by scanning every solicitation opened in the last 24 hours [Kizzy Parks — AHQVro9N9HM @ 00:02:30].

sop_steps.title: Phone for Quotes
sop_steps.action: Call subs on days two and three with the two-question script and collect three to five quotes.
sop_steps.detail: Ask only whether the sub can do the job and what it will cost, and expect a quote within 48 hours [Dr. Wes Fisher — xH6KWT7x8Ac @ 00:02:43]. Collect three to five quotes, preferably local, without assuming geography [Kizzy Parks — kpISY6VCkNY @ 00:01:39].

sop_steps.title: Price in the Middle Band
sop_steps.action: Mark up 7-25% over the sub quote and check the result against the incumbent's price.
sop_steps.detail: A contracting officer put the winning middle at 7-25%, with 10-13% on gravel [Kizzy Parks — etvo2gL7_Cs @ 00:02:23]. If the incumbent charged $2, bid around $2.25 rather than $7-8 [Kizzy Parks — YHptbPFEaPQ @ 00:08:20].

sop_steps.title: Submit and Debrief
sop_steps.action: On day five, submit price, past performance and technical approach, then request a debrief.
sop_steps.detail: 'Nine times out of 10' the government wants price, past performance (yours or your sub's) and a technical approach [Dr. Wes Fisher — xH6KWT7x8Ac @ 00:04:12]. Request a debrief within 3 days of notice; the usual finding is that the price was too high [Kizzy Parks — etvo2gL7_Cs @ 00:04:42].

sections.heading: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The first split is where to sit in the money chain. Sheenapreneur started as a prime on SDVOSB and WOSB status to get paid “straight from the agency,” learned that primes carry payroll before the government pays, and now runs several primes and a couple of subs “as long as the money makes sense”; under $10K, primes usually pay subs upfront while the prime itself waits 30 days [MB8IFp5mwWc @ 00:03:48]. Ricky Howard of GovClose frames the sub seat as relief: the prime owns the proposal, the accounting and getting paid, while the sub builds past performance, and a GovClose client won a nine-figure contract as a subcontractor [z6ZNrmprd-o @ 00:00:37]. Kizzy Parks runs the margin math from the prime seat instead: a prime paid $100 hands Tammy's Toilets $50 and keeps 50%, Tammy spends $5 on equipment and $10 on labor and keeps $35, and the cleaners keep $5 of their $10 and sub out the rest [kpISY6VCkNY @ 00:04:14]. Derek James draws the hard boundary on that stack: limitations on subcontracting apply, and an “illegal pass-through scheme” is fraud [OKLXh8NcJxQ @ 00:03:35]. The operator read: prime when margin and float allow, sub when the vehicle, cash or past performance is missing.

Certifications split the room. Diamond Hunter Enterprises credits the 8(a) and WOSB certification received on January 12, 2017 with the first multimillion-dollar contract, and names 8(a), WOSB, SDVOSB and HUBZone as the doors to set-asides, mentorship and joint ventures [hdZFRp2VG8E @ 00:00:41]. Kizzy Parks says flatly that certifications are not required and builds winners on volume and search discipline instead [ITZqqfI1Eig @ 00:03:38]. The same tension runs through targeting data. Federal Contracts Lab mines USASpending for FY24–26 awards at exactly $14,999 under NAICS 3341, surfacing DoD and Army buyers, but warns that past data is a pattern, not current demand [NUKVGhkCHbg @ 00:11:19]. Parks goes further and rejects USASpending as a predictor, pointing to the infrastructure bill and FAA air-traffic staffing as proof that past purchases do not forecast future ones, and works SAM advanced search on sources sought plus pre-solicitations, roughly 24,000 to 26,000 items, filtered by agency or location down to a Hawaii table rental [ITZqqfI1Eig @ 00:04:11]. Parks also tells operators to respond even after a sources-sought deadline, ask about procurement strategy, and request a capability brief within a couple of weeks. The operator choice: certify when the set-aside pool fits your lane, but source live demand from SAM before trusting historical spend.

Bid tempo and outreach style are the third fault line. Derek James sets the curve at 15 to 20 service bids over a year, calls two or three a week “insane,” and expects bids one through five to be bad, six through ten to improve, and ten through twenty to land “in the money” [OKLXh8NcJxQ @ 00:18:46]. Robert Harvey III ran the opposite tempo: after stalling at one bid a week against a five-a-day goal, Harvey logged about 90 bids since January, roughly a third of them presolicitations, and now pushes two to three a week while Kizzy Parks presses for 12 to 24 contracts [YHptbPFEaPQ @ 00:24:10]. Dr. Wes Fisher compresses a single cycle into five days: list 15 to 20 opportunities on day one, work one to three, get a sub quote inside 48 hours, and submit price, past performance and technical by day five [xH6KWT7x8Ac @ 00:02:17]. On contact, Harvey called one contracting officer 17 times despite Fisher's advice to email, then later kept a buyer warm by emailing a capability statement every two weeks. Pricing bands diverge as well: Parks relays a contracting officer's 7–25% middle with a 10–13% gravel sweet spot, yet allows doubling on upfront-cash, weird or overseas bids [etvo2gL7_Cs @ 00:02:23].

sections.heading: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: Mispricing is the most expensive firsthand failure. Robert Harvey III took a $15K plumbing quote for a Tennessee prison, stacked $20K on top, and watched the contracting officer reject “$335,000 for a two-day job”; Harvey quit for six months, and on a later uniform bid priced shirts at $5 and pants at $7 against rentals costing about 98 cents, landing at $2.2M while Dr. Karen bid $250K over five years [YHptbPFEaPQ @ 00:05:16]. James Walk, 30 to 40 bids in, admits the old reflex was to add $50K and “hit home runs”; the cooling-tower win instead came at a 15% markup on about $42K of parts, under an LPTA award where Walk was not even the lowest bidder [AHQVro9N9HM @ 00:09:21]. Kizzy Parks warns that a 4X tech markup will not be bought, that housekeeping and lawn vendors already bake in 10–30% so adding another 20–50% overbids the job, and that debriefs usually come back with price too high [etvo2gL7_Cs @ 00:04:42]. The trap cuts both ways: Harvey's Colorado contracting officer asked for $1 more per item because the prior vendor priced too low and ghosted [YHptbPFEaPQ @ 00:16:37]. Harvey's own closing warning: don't underbid yourself just to get an award, because it will cost you more than anything.

Winning is not the bottleneck; floating the contract is. Kizzy Parks says winning is easy and the hard part is funding and execution, citing a $155,000 outlay to clear $10,000 in profit [WR8VA1o3VMU @ 00:12:00]. David Packouz hit the same wall at scale: suppliers want payment up front, the government pays “30 days at best” after delivery, and the operator has to float the supplies, the transportation and everything else tied to the contract, which at peak meant three to four aircraft loads of about 45 tons each per week; Packouz's planned fix is an investor bidding system that funds students' won contracts [RrDUfb8vNms @ 00:47:03]. On the livestream, Parks lists the financing walls: business credit carries high interest, you cannot fund against the contract itself, and vendor credit requires references [BZyPDVXuMMk @ 00:42:06]. Derek James sequences the money question: first check whether funding is needed at all, since subs often accept net 30 or paid-when-paid, then budget for a first invoice that may take 60 days, and only then reach for SBA loans or factoring with the cost of money priced into the bid [OKLXh8NcJxQ @ 00:33:18]. Every operator in this chain prices the float before celebrating the margin.

The broker's other exposure is getting cut out or blowing up. Kizzy Parks warns that a prime who fails to project-manage the sub will watch DHS go direct to Tammy's Toilets [kpISY6VCkNY @ 00:07:12], and Derek James lists the government shifting work direct to the sub, FAA staffing cut from 30–50 FTEs to 15–20, and profit concentrated in one CLIN as live pricing risks [OKLXh8NcJxQ @ 00:35:17]. Ricky Howard's defense is to never send a prospective partner the link or exact opportunity, only generalities [z6ZNrmprd-o @ 00:05:28]. The extreme case is David Packouz: a just-under-$300M munitions award, then Chinese-origin ammunition the contract barred directly or indirectly, a choice to repackage rather than request a waiver, 71 aircraft loads producing 71 certificates of conformance and a 355-year exposure, seven months of house arrest for Packouz, four years for the partner, about $500K in fines and a ban of roughly 15 years [RrDUfb8vNms @ 00:27:32]. Packouz adds that the Army knew the origin and kept taking delivery for six more months, about $30M worth. Packouz's rules from the wreckage: put partners on legally binding agreements, after being offered a $100K salary plus 1% in place of a 25% profit share, and never write an email you would not want read out in court or published in the newspaper.

callout.title: Four Checks Before Any Bid Goes Out
callout.body: Run every bid through these four checks before submission; each one maps to a loss, reversal or near-miss a named operator lived through.
items: Price against the market, not ambition: pull FPDS awards (2024 roofing ran about 12,000 to 21,000 against a $1M estimate that “may be off”) and stay in the 7–25% band unless the bid is upfront-cash, weird or overseas [Kizzy Parks — etvo2gL7_Cs @ 00:03:13].

Confirm the float before bidding: match supplier terms to government terms the way James Walk paired distributor net 30 with government net 30 and bid within means [Kizzy Parks — AHQVro9N9HM @ 00:11:31].
Protect the deal before teaming: give prospective partners generalities only and never send the link or exact opportunity [GovClose | DoD Contract Academy — z6ZNrmprd-o @ 00:05:28].

Verify the item is sourceable and profitable: on DIBBS check NSN, quantity and due date, ask whether you can still profit, and beware approved-source items [Federal Contracts Lab — NUKVGhkCHbg @ 00:18:36].

Phone subs on days two and three with two questions only, can you do the job and how much will it cost, and expect a quote inside 48 hours [Dr. Wes Fisher — xH6KWT7x8Ac @ 00:02:55].
Collect three to five sub quotes, preferably local, without assuming geography rules out a national provider such as a New Mexico firm [Kizzy Parks — kpISY6VCkNY @ 00:01:39].
Answer sources sought and pre-solicitations even after the deadline, ask about procurement strategy, and request a capability brief within a couple of weeks [Kizzy Parks — ITZqqfI1Eig @ 00:08:52].
Request a debrief within three days of the award notice and expect the usual finding to be a price that was too high [Kizzy Parks — etvo2gL7_Cs @ 00:04:42].
Build a 60/40 pipeline of one-and-done and long-term work, tracked in Excel tabs per set-aside from SAM advanced searches [Kizzy Parks — DAbMwnUtgfI @ 00:08:53].

chapters.question_prompt: How do I use set-asides to target opportunities, and where do I find state, local and cooperative purchasing bids?
chapters.title: Targeting Set-Asides and State, Local and Cooperative Bids
chapters.subtitle: When to apply for set-asides, searching SAM.gov by set-aside, getting more WOSB, SDVOSB and HUBZone set-asides, whether SDVOSB helps you win, finding county, city, school and Texas bids, weekly SLED opportunity breakdowns, bid sites, and Sourcewell cooperative contracts
chapters.executive_summary: Practitioners agree that state, local, school and cooperative buying is softer ground than the federal portal. It brings less competition, easier registration, local preference, and co-op awards that replace a year-long RFP with a priced quote. On federal set-asides, they agree the certification narrows the field but never delivers the work. Outreach does: sources-sought responses, contracting-officer calls, and team campaigns. The numbers they use are concrete. Texas SmartBuy drops from 20,000 pages to 27 once filtered. New Jersey quote thresholds run $17,500 to $53,000. An SDVOSB search narrows from 61 to 14 results with a Sources Sought filter. Twenty to 30 sources-sought responses yield 5 to 10 RFP responses. Janitorial work is priced per service point. They split on timing: one camp files certifications early, while others wait for prime wins, and one veteran operator says veteran status alone moves nothing.

sections.heading: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every SLED-focused operator starts from the same premise: state, county, city and school-district buying is softer ground than the federal portal. SamSearch argues local work carries less competition than sam.gov, relaxed registration, a proximity edge, and the chance to stack in-state past performance [OmEqzgzoKlc @ 00:00:31]. It makes the same case for cities, which buy everything from cleaning to jiu-jitsu classes and lean toward local businesses over past performance [RY7zan9X3oY @ 00:01:40]. The same channel names the friction plainly: every city runs its own site and its own process, so the edge goes to whoever maps the portals first. Win the Bid frames the entry ramp around thresholds. Below the formal-bid line the goal is getting called for quotes, while bigger purchases go out as formal public bids [roNNP4jeQpc @ 00:00:55]. The Government Contracting Strategist & Host adds the discipline side: "don't chase the map, choose a lane." That advice came in a week that surfaced 12,441 new opportunities nationwide, and the host flagged a $13,000 records-scanning job as the kind of small contract that opens doors [-S6wZyOulKA @ 00:02:54]. The consensus playbook is to pick a geography and a trade, register on the free local portals, and work the small, recurring buys before chasing marquee awards.

On cooperative contracts, suppliers, a dealer and Sourcewell itself tell one story: the solicitation work is already done. Wheelen bid and won a Sourcewell award directly, then authorized US and Canadian distributors. Agencies simply pick a distributor and "cut out the bid process" [511aPYJ9WjI @ 00:01:00]. Foley Equipment runs the same mechanic from the dealer seat. Caterpillar won the national solicitation, cities buy straight from the Cat dealer, and a priced quote goes to council with no RFP or RFQ cycle [Hlnggncm3KQ @ 00:01:06]. Foley puts cooperative purchasing at roughly 20-30% of US purchases and says salespeople and city officials often don't know it exists, so Foley educates commissions and boards. Crosby Grindle of Provident has about 20 years in co-op buying. Grindle says co-op contracts satisfy the highest procurement tier and replace a conventional RFP that takes "a year or more." Buyers also keep their local supplier while getting national pricing [V3qc9e4w-4M @ 00:14:30]. Sourcewell's own fire-apparatus pitch matches: a traditional bid can add up to a year, while co-op means "most of that work's done for you" [vTX0ljZ_Nro @ 00:00:42]. The operator takeaway every one of them repeats is that once the award exists, the sale becomes a quote, not a bid, and the person who explains the contract vehicle to the board controls the deal.

On federal set-asides, the agreement is blunter: the badge narrows the field but never delivers the work. Rick Howard of GovClose is an ex-acquisitions officer who reports managing $82B in DoD contracts. Howard warns that the certification won't win contracts; the product or service will, and nothing will "land in your lap" [Qij-5QQmwc8 @ 00:03:05]. GovKidMethod reaches the same verdict on 8(a): "The SBA is not going to be bringing you contracts," so the advice is to wait until one or two prime contracts are in hand [xXM1cyLQ_jY @ 00:07:09]. Where speakers align is the math that makes set-asides worth targeting anyway. US Federal Contractor Registration lays out goals of 23% small business, 5% for minority, women and 8(a), 3% SDVOSB, and 3% HUBZone. In that breakdown, 69,000 WOSBs and 62,000 minority firms split their 5%, while 16,000 SDVOSBs share an extra 3% [yFsBD592FN8 @ 00:06:51]. Neil McDonnell's FY2023 count shows how thin each pool is: 11,152 SDVOSB, 2,845 WOSB, 1,534 HUBZone, and 872 8(a) set-aside awards out of 5,413,622 new contracts [4poj2n7iLrs @ 00:00:58]. The shared baseline is SAM registration, a matching size standard, and then direct outreach that turns a certification into an actual set-aside tag on a real requirement.

sections.heading: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: The SLED search grind is concrete. On Texas SmartBuy, SamSearch shows an unfiltered view of "20,000 pages," then cuts it down by searching one keyword and setting status to "posted." Even with no keyword, the posted filter drops the list to 27 pages [OmEqzgzoKlc @ 00:02:43]. Win the Bid works New Jersey by the LFN 2025-08 thresholds, effective July 1, 2025. The limits are $17,500 for towns and counties without a qualified purchasing agent, $39,000 for school districts without one, and up to $53,000 with one. Legal notices must run at least 10 days before bids are due [roNNP4jeQpc @ 00:00:33]. New York's State Contract Reporter carries $50K-plus work, registration is free, and alerts do the watching. Pennsylvania runs through COSTARS, and the weekly routine includes 15 minutes of checking and calling the purchasing office. D'S Construction runs five Louisiana sites every morning: SAM.gov, LaPAC for state agencies, Central Bidding for cities, parishes and school boards, Centerline Bid Connect for LSU construction, and MyBidMatch through the APEX Accelerator. Damian works South Louisiana jobs under $50,000 and set-asides first [yxjYYFbCa5E @ 00:02:40]. Central Bidding documents and plan-holder lists cost about $110/month, and the free workaround is a paper copy from the clerk or school board [yxjYYFbCa5E @ 00:01:39].

For federal set-asides, the mechanics start in the search filter. GovKidMethod uses the set-aside filter in Contract Opportunities. SDVOSB plus a NAICS code returned 61 results, and adding "Sources Sought" narrowed it to 14. That list becomes market research before paying for any certification [nRXCetmIWUs @ 00:02:09]. Neil McDonnell turns those notices into set-asides with a five-step campaign [4poj2n7iLrs @ 00:22:58]:
1. Pick a low-friction opportunity that was full-and-open or total small business, not an 8(a) incumbent.
2. Call the contracting officer for 15-20 minutes.
3. Contact the agency's small-business professional.
4. Build a team of 10-20 firms.
5. Have each firm respond to the sources-sought notice requesting one tag only.
On the rule of two, McDonnell says "forget about it": 20-30 sources-sought responses yield 5-10 RFP responses. McDonnell's proof points: the 2018 set-aside calls helped move an extra $3B to HUBZone firms, and about 100 firms answering the State Department in one day produced a $200M set-aside. Rick Howard runs the same front end. Howard targets sources-sought notices and RFIs, pushes set-asides plus requirements such as PMP or CISSP, and backs every claim with metrics, never fabrications [Qij-5QQmwc8 @ 00:54:12]. One RFI Howard walked through capped responses at 15 pages, so the pitch has to be tight.

Pricing and ordering mechanics close the loop. The Government Contracting Strategist & Host prices janitorial work by service point, not square foot: take the last job's price and divide it by visits, restrooms, or stops [iTD46ZpHbdI @ 00:16:25]. The same host reads bid tabs and award letters. One example is an NCDOT US-70 rest area last awarded at $111,648 to the lowest responsible bid, with the rule "price against history and not just guess at it" [iTD46ZpHbdI @ 00:10:32]. On simplified acquisitions, US Federal Contractor Registration reports that one quote is allowed when the price is fair against FPDS history. Agencies may prepay a deposit, half, or the full amount. An FPDS demo turned up a $10,000 award paid in full upfront with 4 offers, and a $45,000 SAP award with "no competition" [yFsBD592FN8 @ 00:05:43]. For co-op orders, Provident's Ryan Donovan says Sourcewell registration carries no cost or obligation and lasts for life. Group benefits still need a quote, and the PO must cite the agency account number and the contract number [V3qc9e4w-4M @ 00:30:12]. Donovan puts Sourcewell at about $1B in annual sales across 700+ suppliers and 50,000+ registered agencies. Grindle adds that sales through co-op contracts overall are almost $60B.

sections.heading: 3. Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The loudest split on this circuit is when to chase set-aside paper. GovKidMethod openly rejects the industry dogma of stacking certifications the moment SAM registration clears [xXM1cyLQ_jY @ 00:00:15]. Their sequencing is surgical: grab WOSB or EDWOSB soon after SAM because it costs little time, but hold off on 8(a), a nine-year program that normally demands two years in business and tax returns, until the firm has one or two prime contracts under its belt [xXM1cyLQ_jY @ 00:06:36]. SamSearch frames the same program as worth going through, pitching 8(a) sole-source awards up to $4.5M, or $7M in manufacturing, against a 51% disadvantaged-ownership and two-year bar [PPOCeCEkaBk @ 00:04:57]. The two camps are not arguing about whether 8(a) pays. They are arguing about whether a firm with no federal track record should start its nine-year clock before it has anything to sell into it. Rick Howard of GovClose, an ex-acquisitions officer who says he managed $82B in DoD contracts, cuts across both camps: the certification will not win contracts, the product or service will [Qij-5QQmwc8 @ 00:03:05]. The operator takeaway is to treat each certificate as a multiplier on an existing offer, sequenced by approval speed, not as an entry ticket.

On the veteran and HUBZone lanes, the practitioners read the same federal data and reach different temperatures. Rick Howard drills USASpending to show the VA sending over 90% of its awards in architecture, engineering and construction codes to SDVOSB or veteran set-asides, and tells uncertified firms to avoid those agencies outright [Qij-5QQmwc8 @ 00:13:41]. He also argues that plain veteran-owned status, without the service-disabled certification, does not move the needle at all [Qij-5QQmwc8 @ 00:24:43]. GovKidMethod sits at 50/50 on SDVOSB timing, citing a three-to-six-month VA certification timeline while waving off consultants who charge $2-3K for little added value. HUBZone produces the sharpest contrast. GovKidMethod warns there are few HUBZone set-aside opportunities, up to six months to certify, and an employee-residency ratio a growing firm can outgrow, so do not pursue it early [xXM1cyLQ_jY @ 00:14:21]. Neil McDonnell flips the problem from supply to demand: the 2018 set-aside calls helped move an extra $3B to HUBZone firms, and at the State Department about 100 firms responded in a single day, which led to a $200M set-aside [4poj2n7iLrs @ 00:11:57]. One camp waits for set-asides to appear; the other organizes firms to create them.

Cooperative purchasing splits the room on framing. Foley Equipment sells Sourcewell to commissions and boards as a shortcut: Caterpillar already won the national solicitation, so a priced quote goes straight to council with no RFP or RFQ process [Hlnggncm3KQ @ 00:01:06]. FDIC International pitches the Wheelen contract the same way, saying agencies choose their distributor and cut out the bid process [511aPYJ9WjI @ 00:01:00]. Provident's webinar draws a hard line against that language: never pitch a co-op contract as a way to get around procurement. Instead, position it as satisfying the highest procurement tier because a lead agency already ran the competition, and tell buyers to read their own policy for best-value versus lowest-price authority [V3qc9e4w-4M @ 00:19:43]. The SLED hunters split on breadth. The Government Contracting Strategist & Host tells newcomers not to chase the map but to choose a lane, while SamSearch sells AI coverage of about 300 procurement sites. D'S Construction checks five bid sites every morning, working South Louisiana jobs under $50,000 and set-asides first [yxjYYFbCa5E @ 00:02:40]. Win the Bid splits the difference with a five-step routine that budgets 15 minutes a week to checking boards and calling the purchasing office.

sections.heading: 4. Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most expensive trap the federal practitioners report is waiting for a certificate to deliver revenue. Rick Howard is blunt that contracts will not land in your lap after certification, even though the SDVOSB approval took about two weeks while 8(a) and WOSB can run far longer [Qij-5QQmwc8 @ 00:03:39]. GovKidMethod lands on the same point from the SBA side: the SBA is not going to be bringing you contracts, which is why 8(a) should wait until real prime past performance exists [xXM1cyLQ_jY @ 00:07:09]. Certification can also slip out from under a firm. HUBZone eligibility hangs on an employee-residency ratio, with 35% of employees required to live in a HUBZone per US Federal Contractor Registration, so a firm that hires outside the zone can outgrow its own status [xXM1cyLQ_jY @ 00:13:48]. A quieter trap is assuming a state badge travels: GovKidMethod warns that state WOSB certification is not the same as federal [nRXCetmIWUs @ 00:02:42], and that federal WOSB is no longer self-certified. Neil McDonnell's numbers show the gap: about 95K self-certified WOSBs exist against 11-12K SBA-certified, and WOSBs won $27B while less than $1B was actually set aside for them.

On the state and local side, the failures are procedural and they are final. D'S Construction flags the mandatory pre-bid meeting: miss it and you can't submit [yxjYYFbCa5E @ 00:02:56]. The same episode exposes the paywall trap on Central Bidding, where cities, parishes and school boards post for free browsing but documents and plan-holder lists sit behind a subscription of about $110 a month. The workaround is a paper copy from the clerk or school board [yxjYYFbCa5E @ 00:01:07]. For subcontractors, that plan-holder list is the gold because it shows which GCs will receive your number. SamSearch names fragmentation as the core bottleneck of city work: every city has its own site and its own process, which is the pain its aggregation and AI summaries are built to absorb [RY7zan9X3oY @ 00:02:30]. Then there is scope that bleeds margin after award. Breaking down Miami-Dade's nightly bus cleaning, the Government Contracting Strategist & Host tells bidders to own the night shift with depot access and a 2 a.m. supervisor, but to price the on-call daytime piece carefully because that is where contractors get burned [iTD46ZpHbdI @ 00:07:46].

The economics checks come down to history and time. The Government Contracting Strategist & Host hammers one rule: price against history and not just guess at it, reading bid tabs and award letters. The last NCDOT US-70 rest-area award went to the lowest responsible bid at $111,648 [iTD46ZpHbdI @ 00:10:32]. For janitorial, the same host prices by service point rather than square foot, dividing the last job's price by visits, restrooms or stops, and splits daily work from event surge so the contracting officer isn't guessing. Time is the second check. Rick Howard tells operators to plan six to eighteen months to a first win [Qij-5QQmwc8 @ 00:43:57], and warns that reported award data lags, so a peer firm's trajectory of $2.5M to $16.4M to $16.1M deserves skepticism [Qij-5QQmwc8 @ 00:37:47]. On the co-op side, Provident puts a conventional RFP process at a year or more, and Sourcewell Gov says a traditional apparatus bid can add up to a year, the cycle cooperative purchasing is sold to skip [V3qc9e4w-4M @ 00:18:57]. US Federal Contractor Registration adds the counterweight on small buys: a $45,000 simplified acquisition drew no competition, and a $10,000 award was paid in full upfront.

chapters.question_prompt: How do I find what the government paid before, read demand data, and build a defensible price?
chapters.title: Pricing Intelligence and Cost Buildup
chapters.subtitle: Past award prices from FPDS and USASpending.gov, award history for recompetes, finding WOSB set-asides in FPDS, DLA DIBBS demand, direct and indirect costs (fringe, overhead, G&A, wrap rates), FAR 31 cost support, FAR 12/15 pricing, and FAR 15 negotiation
chapters.executive_summary: Practitioners converge on one rule: never price a federal bid blind. Kizzy Parks, Fox Wade, FedAccess and Neil McDonnell pull incumbent award values out of FPDS, USAspending, GSA eLibrary and direct POC emails, then work backwards from term length and evaluation criteria. Solvability's cost team builds the other half of the number: fringe near 30%, G&A at an 8-15% norm, a client-site wrap rate near 1.5 versus the Reagan-era 2.0 multiplier, and a 5-10% fee. FAR-side speakers add the hard lines: certified cost or pricing data above $2M, allocable and supportable costs, and unallowables kept out of every pool. Tension remains over how low to go: Parks priced so low a contracting office asked if it was an error and won, Bobby Butler breaks even on the first 1-12 DLA awards, while Solvability warns underbid fringe loses money.

sections.heading: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every pricing practitioner in this lineup starts from the same premise: the last price the government paid is public, and bidding without it is how owners burn money. Fox Wade admits their early pricing was off by $4-5M and once by $15M, and their answer is to pull what the government already paid out of free public data before touching a bid number [Z2ZeI5rayvk @ 00:00:37]. FedAccess opens with an owner who spent heavily chasing a contract that turned out to be worth only a couple hundred thousand dollars, not millions, then walks the fix through SAM.gov and FPDS step by step [GrYP5KyxBho @ 00:01:29]. Kizzy Parks makes it a standing habit: on every sources sought, RFI, RFQ or solicitation, email the POC and ask whether there is an incumbent, its name, its contract number and its contract value [L0SM3XAM3IE @ 00:00:24]. Neil McDonnell frames FPDS as roughly 80% of where a contractor's activity should live, covering what they estimate is ninety-plus percent of awards and excluding only classified buys and purchases at or under $10,000 [17foq325L5w @ 00:04:57]. The shared logic is that pricing intelligence and pipeline intelligence come out of the same records, so the operator who mines award history wins twice: once on target selection and again on the number written into the bid, before a single labor rate is built.

The second point of agreement is that the price paid is only a reference until the evaluation criteria tell you how to use it. Kizzy Parks puts it bluntly: knowing the price is great, but the evaluation criteria always rule; on a lowest-cost award with a $500K prior, come in around that or lower, while technical-led awards turn the old price into a rough guide [L0SM3XAM3IE @ 00:02:44]. Carrie, the Colorado government contracts lawyer with 25 years in the field, draws the same line in FAR Part 15 terms: LPTA makes technical pass/fail with no trade-off, while best value must still evaluate price and generally past performance [Tj7x3UDuOSE @ 00:12:51]. On the cost side, Solvability's Jenny says price must be as low as reasonable or you are just going to lose, and even a best-value buyer needs a reason to pay more [lOumu-Dk0Jw @ 00:02:09]. Ellen Beebe, after 33 years in estimating and pricing, splits the market in two: commercial items under Part 12 are priced to what the market will bear against competitors' similar items, while Part 15 sole-source proposals over $2M demand certified cost or pricing data backed by a bill of materials consolidated across every line item [SpRIyXgvkg0 @ 00:01:06]. Every speaker treats the final number as a function of the evaluation method and the buying vehicle, never of what the contractor would like to charge.

The baseline prerequisite the cost-side speakers share is a books-and-records system that can defend the number after award. Solvability's Johnny Clark, a fractional GovCon CFO, tells contractors to book the way they bill, pointing to DCAA's SF 1408 checklist, and to run GAAP accrual books with a monthly close by the 15th to 20th, direct and indirect costs separated, and interest expense booked as unallowable [EBQwejU6UUQ @ 00:05:37]. GovSuccess reduces FAR 31.201-2 to five conditions that all have to pass: reasonableness, allocability, accounting standards, contract terms and cost-principle limits, warning that clearing one does not settle the rest and that an indirect-cost pool never makes an unallowable expense disappear [i7_rrrRpotk @ 00:01:10]. That lines up with Jenny's unallowable list: interest, alcohol, entertainment, first-class airfare, lobbying, gifts, contributions and advertising [lOumu-Dk0Jw @ 00:09:52]. Carrie adds that certified cost or pricing data must be facts, must include all sub quotes, and must disclose profit or fee plus overhead and G&A, including the parent company's, with no exemption for small businesses [Tj7x3UDuOSE @ 00:17:35]. The consensus is that intelligence gets you to a competitive number, but only clean timekeeping, a segregated chart of accounts and documented allocations let you keep the money once an auditor or contracting officer starts asking questions.

sections.heading: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Fox Wade's extraction routine is the cleanest on record: copy the incumbent contract number into FPDS, sort by date signed, ignore the latest modification (theirs showed 348k), and scroll down to modification 0 for the base award, which revealed an August 2020 award running Sep 28 to Sep 27 2023, not a set-aside, not a BPA, totaling $1,686,566.88 over three years [Z2ZeI5rayvk @ 00:02:50]. FedAccess runs the same date-signed sort on a Seeley Lake janitorial recompete with a base year plus four options and lands on $47,352.42 for 3/10/2020 to 9/30/2024, plus the incumbent's contact details and the number of bids received [GrYP5KyxBho @ 00:03:56]. Neil McDonnell insists on field-specific search rather than bare keywords, which USAspending cannot match, then targets 100 to 200 results with a ceiling of 500, sorts by action obligation or date signed, and exports CSV against a roughly 5,000-row limit, never PDF because there is no value in it [0cGdQvymmvY @ 00:25:43]. In the WOSB walkthrough they read a $146K action as probably around $1M total and a $2M action as possibly $10M, and they ignore anything under $1M when hunting [YR_aPfXedtA @ 00:15:26]. The repeatable mechanic is always the same: find the base action, rebuild the term and total, and only then decide where your number lands against the incumbent.

For labor rates, Kizzy Parks calls GSA eLibrary their number one intel tip: it shows which schedules an incumbent or competitor holds, such as a JV on STARS III and two firms on MAS, along with posted rates like 63.52 for specialists and labor category descriptions you can borrow to craft your own [L0SM3XAM3IE @ 00:13:57]. On buy.gsa.gov a contract-number search failed, but a Project Manager II lookup averaged 143 with a 103 to 183 range, and the floor of 60 tied to a bachelor's degree and six years of experience, so a candidate with ten years justifies a higher rate [L0SM3XAM3IE @ 00:11:49]. SamSearch works USAspending the same way, keyword-searching award descriptions such as website development to surface historical values, then filtering by the incumbent's ID to see everything that firm has been paid [NiWdxgnr3xo @ 00:12:51]. Eric Coffie's bulk version filters FY2019 and FY2018 plus a state, downloads the file, and builds an Excel pivot table to sort the fields into a usable rate and award picture [Hr_U9z1xK2g @ 00:00:59]. Stacked together, these four pulls give an operator a defensible labor-rate band, a list of who is charging what, and the exact category language buyers already accept, all before a single proposal page gets drafted or a wrap rate is applied.

Solvability's Jenny builds the burden in FOG order, fringe then overhead then G&A, with fringe equal to payroll costs over productive labor, overhead equal to overhead costs over direct labor, and G&A equal to corporate costs over total cost input [lOumu-Dk0Jw @ 00:31:40]. Fringe runs about 30%: payroll taxes near 10% (bid 5% and you lose money), leave of 200 out of 2,080 hours, and traps like 88 holiday hours instead of 80 or 56 hours of SCA/EO sick leave. The old 2.0 multiplier, $50 to $100, dates to the Reagan years; at a client site, 30% fringe, 3% overhead, 8% G&A and 7% fee lands near 1.5, so $50 becomes about $75, and competitors may target 1.45 [lOumu-Dk0Jw @ 00:40:51]. Run it backwards and a $75 bill rate caps pay at about $48. Johnny Clark adds that a strong growth forecast can drop G&A, so you don't need to bid 40% G&A [EBQwejU6UUQ @ 00:00:35]. On the product side, Bobby Butler prices landed cost: a $10 flashlight in 2025 can cost $13 in 2026 once tariffs, logistics, packaging and shipping are added, so $10 plus 15% is the wrong math [6Fz712e3oWc @ 00:24:31]. Fee stays modest across the board, with Jenny calling 5-10% good and noting you won't see 12-15%.

callout.title: Pricing Intel Shortcuts the Practitioners Actually Use
callout.body: Four small habits that separate operators who price from data from operators who price from hope.
items: Share and save FPDS searches by URL: the query lives in the URL, so copy it and send it to a teammate instead of rebuilding filters [Neil McDonnell — 17foq325L5w @ 00:25:07]

Never guess a withheld value: Kizzy Parks assumed an Army award was at least $250K and it came in around $35K, so ask the POC for incumbent, contract number and value every time [Kizzy Parks — L0SM3XAM3IE @ 00:05:28]
Pull the old solicitation alongside the award: in SAM.gov use exact phrase with Status set to Inactive, because scope can grow from 2 people to 10 [FedAccess — GrYP5KyxBho @ 00:05:33]
When a cost is gray-area, put it in overhead rather than G&A, or your G&A rate goes through the roof and you won't win any business [Solvability — lOumu-Dk0Jw @ 00:27:28]

sop_steps.title: Extract incumbent identity and value
sop_steps.action: Email the POC on every sources sought, RFI, RFQ or solicitation asking for incumbent name, contract number and contract value.
sop_steps.detail: Skip the email only when an attachment already names the incumbent and value, then work backwards to the term behind the number (1, 2.5, 3 or 5 years) [Kizzy Parks — L0SM3XAM3IE @ 00:00:24]

sop_steps.action: Paste the incumbent contract number into FPDS, sort by date signed, and open modification 0.
sop_steps.detail: Read award date, start and end dates, set-aside and BPA status, and total value; Fox Wade's base award showed $1,686,566.88 over three years while the latest action showed only 348k [Fox Wade — Z2ZeI5rayvk @ 00:02:50]

sop_steps.title: Benchmark labor rates
sop_steps.action: Search the labor category on buy.gsa.gov and the incumbent's schedules on GSA eLibrary.
sop_steps.detail: Record the average, range and floor (Project Manager II averaged 143 across 103-183, floor of 60 at six years' experience) and adjust for your candidates' experience [Kizzy Parks — L0SM3XAM3IE @ 00:11:49]

sop_steps.title: Wrap and back-solve the rate
sop_steps.action: Apply fringe, overhead, G&A and fee in FOG order in an Excel wrap calculator, then run it backwards from the target bill rate.
sop_steps.detail: At a client site expect roughly a 1.5 wrap; a $75 bill rate means you can't pay more than about $48, so set pay from the competitive bill rate rather than the reverse [Solvability — lOumu-Dk0Jw @ 00:42:07]

sections.heading: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split is over how hard to cut price. Solvability's Jenny compares indirect rates to taxes, using a downtown Atlanta dealer analogy, and says price must be as low as reasonable "or else you're just going to lose," while conceding that best value still needs a reason to pay more [lOumu-Dk0Jw @ 00:02:09]. Kizzy Parks refuses to let the number drive the bid by itself: "the evaluation criteria always rules." A $500K lowest-cost prior award means coming in at or under that figure, while a technically weighted buy only uses price as a rough guide [L0SM3XAM3IE @ 00:02:44]. On an Air Force exercise physiologist LPTA, they priced so low that contracting asked whether they had made an error, and they still won because they knew the profit they could keep. Carrie, a 25-year government contracts lawyer, pushes back on the race to zero: "Profit is good." Fee caps only bite on cost-plus-fixed-fee deals, at 15% for R&D and 10% otherwise, and sole-source awards simply get negotiated harder [Tj7x3UDuOSE @ 00:35:22]. Bobby Butler of myContractScout runs a third line on DLA buys. Break even or take a thin margin on the first one to twelve awards purely to build CPARS history, then price for profit [6Fz712e3oWc @ 00:17:49].

Practitioners also split on which rates belong in the bid. Johnny Clark, a fractional GovCon CFO at Solvability, tells operators to price on forecast: if growth will dilute corporate cost, you "don't need to bid 40% G&A" today [EBQwejU6UUQ @ 00:00:35]. Jenny sets rates per calendar year and acknowledges they fall as the company scales, yet assumes flat rates across three-to-five-year forecasts [lOumu-Dk0Jw @ 00:29:37]. Jenny also retires the old rule of thumb. A 2.0 multiplier that turns $50 of pay into a $100 bill rate dates to "the Reagan years." A client-site staffing shop should run about 1.5, built from 30% fringe, 3% overhead, 8% G&A and 7% fee, and competitors may target 1.45 [lOumu-Dk0Jw @ 00:40:51]. The pricing method itself forks by FAR part. Ellen Beebe, with 33 years in estimating, says Part 15 sole-source proposals over $2M demand certified cost or pricing data, including a bill of materials consolidated across every line item. Part 12 commercial items are priced to what the market will bear, off competitors' similar items [SpRIyXgvkg0 @ 00:01:06]. Carrie adds that certification is prohibited below the $250,000 SAT and required above $2M and on modifications above $750K. Adequate competition and commercial items are exempt [Tj7x3UDuOSE @ 00:20:51].

The intel stack is contested too. Neil McDonnell calls FPDS "80% of your activity, or it should be," and builds two-year recompete pipelines almost entirely from it, sizing $25-100M in opportunities to land $5M in revenue [17foq325L5w @ 00:11:22]. SamSearch counters that USAspending is free, easier than SAM, and covers $6.8T a year, making it the place to pull historical award values by keyword and incumbent ID [NiWdxgnr3xo @ 00:12:51]. Kizzy Parks prefers FPDS but leaned on paid GovWin for the Air Force pricing, distrusts SAM archives, and cross-checks GovTribe trials. They call GSA eLibrary rate sheets their "number one tip" for intel [L0SM3XAM3IE @ 00:13:57]. Kizzy also works the small end of the market. GovWin showed Catholic youth coordinator awards running from about $17K to $40-50K, and a 20-50% profit on those still pays well. Bobby Butler rejects paid lead feeds outright. A $3,000-a-month list resold to 25 to 100 companies triggers a race to the bottom, and switching to the free DLA No Bid List saves $36,000 a year [6Fz712e3oWc @ 00:04:15]. Everyone here mines federal award data, but they split on which database leads, which dollar floor matters, and whether a paid layer earns its fee.

sections.heading: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The costliest misses start with misread award data. Fox Wade admits their early pricing was off by $4-5M, and once by $15M. The fix was to pull the incumbent's FPDS record, sort by date signed, and scroll to modification 0 for the base award [Z2ZeI5rayvk @ 00:00:37]. That step matters because the latest action showed only $348K while the base award totaled $1,686,566.88 over three years [Z2ZeI5rayvk @ 00:02:50]. FedAccess opens with an owner who spent heavily chasing a contract worth only "a couple hundred thousand." They also warn that scope can jump from 2 people to 10, so the old solicitation must be pulled before trusting the $47,352.42 price [GrYP5KyxBho @ 00:05:33]. Kizzy Parks got burned when the Army withheld the value: they assumed at least $250K, and the award came in around $35K [L0SM3XAM3IE @ 00:05:28]. Neil McDonnell flags the opposite trap. Completion dates mislead because of option years, and a $146K obligation is probably about $1M total, while $2M could be $10M [YR_aPfXedtA @ 00:15:26]. Kizzy's counter is to work backwards on term every time, because a $2M value means something very different over one, three, or five years.

On the buildup side, Jenny warns that payroll taxes alone run about 10%. Bidding 5% fringe means "you're going to lose money cuz you haven't covered everything," and a 60% G&A puts a firm out of the game against an 8-15% norm [lOumu-Dk0Jw @ 00:13:16]. Their own worked example uses $10M revenue with 30% fringe, 38.35% overhead, 10% G&A and 8% profit, and they flag those rates as too high to win [lOumu-Dk0Jw @ 00:35:09]. Johnny Clark's DCAA fail test is a single $300,000 wages line. Labor distribution must tie to gross payroll, timesheet changes need an audit trail, and a bill for 170 PM hours must trace back to daily time recording [EBQwejU6UUQ @ 00:17:14]. GovSuccess shows the allocation trap with a $2,000 shared test-equipment invoice across four projects. Dumping it on one job is wrong, equal splits are not automatic, and one-quarter usage points to a $500 allocation to investigate [i7_rrrRpotk @ 00:02:29]. They add that "an indirect-cost pool does not make an unallowable expense disappear." Bobby Butler's landed-cost lesson closes the loop. A $10 flashlight in 2025 can cost $13 in 2026 after tariffs, logistics, packaging and shipping, so "$10 + 15%" is the wrong math [6Fz712e3oWc @ 00:24:31].

Execution traps hit after the number is set. Bobby Butler watched an awardee fail to meet the delivery date and names the repeat mistakes: not verifying the item is still open, ignoring delivery dates, bidding without a supplier, omitting freight and tariffs, and skipping FOB and inspection clauses [6Fz712e3oWc @ 00:25:46]. The No Bid List is a 10-20K item snapshot with some lines already awarded or cancelled, and quoting 10 cents instead of $10 still obligates you if the award is made [6Fz712e3oWc @ 00:30:01]. Carrie lays out the Part 15 tripwires: "late is late," an accepted late proposal stays protestable, and a withdrawn proposal cannot be resubmitted [Tj7x3UDuOSE @ 00:22:09]. Defective pricing brings price adjustments, fees, interest, penalties, CPARS damage, and possible criminal or civil exposure [Tj7x3UDuOSE @ 00:50:04]. Neil McDonnell adds a research bottleneck. FPDS holds summary data only, with no PWS or scope documents, so the work statement has to come from SAM, the CO, or FOIA [0cGdQvymmvY @ 00:10:10]. Johnny Clark warns that CPAs are "general practitioners," so the books behind a cost buildup need a GovCon specialist rather than a generalist [EBQwejU6UUQ @ 00:31:06].

callout.body: Clear all four checks before any number leaves the building.
items: Pull modification 0 and the old solicitation before pricing a recompete, because the latest action and changed scope both distort the number [Fox Wade — Z2ZeI5rayvk @ 00:02:50].

chapters.question_prompt: How do I break down an RFP, RFQ or RFI and produce a compliant proposal quickly?
chapters.title: Responding to Solicitations and Building Compliant Proposals
chapters.subtitle: RFI vs. RFQ vs. RFP, Section L/M breakdowns, building compliance matrices step by step and with AI, the clarification process, a janitorial RFP walkthrough, AI-assisted 4-hour responses, proposal tools, and bid-window programs
chapters.executive_summary: Practitioners agree on one law: responsiveness is unforgiving. Bids die at the contracting officer's first gate review on font, page and missing-item non-compliance, well before price matters. The answer is a compliance matrix built before kickoff. It pulls out every shall, must and will, then maps each one to a volume and page, an owner, a status and a Section M evaluation factor. Shannon Lindauer reports 4-10 hours per matrix and an 83% win rate. Promptly cuts the work to four AI prompts at $9.99/month. Point2Pivot drafted a roughly $224K DFO bid in Claude after ChatGPT came back 'very light.' The core mechanics are page budgets weighted by evaluation score, crosswalk headings, seasonal janitorial pricing, and submitting early, because 12:01 for a noon deadline is rejected. Practitioners split on Word versus Excel, on executive summaries, and on how far to trust AI output that invents figures.

sections.title: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Operators agree on where proposals die. It is not at price; it is at the contracting officer's first gate review. Shannon Lindauer of The Federal Proposal Experts says many offerors are eliminated there for font, outline or missing-content non-compliance. That is why she calls the compliance matrix the most important document a bid team can create [zeJUuxLmj6s @ 00:01:03]. Bid and Comply opens with the same verdict: most tenders are not lost on price. It defines the matrix as a record of every requirement with its location, evidence and owner [c73xWsLDDhc @ 00:00:00]. The Illinois APEX Accelerator director at CHCEDC states it as a hard rule: in a bid, responsiveness is unforgiving. GAO enforces page and font limits, and proposing exceptions can make you non-responsive [46vBsddH6zQ @ 00:58:15]. Virtual 24-7 drives it home for first-timers. Missing even one required item can get a proposal thrown out, and a DBE set-aside shuts out non-certified firms before they start [yH2TsdfzuTM @ 00:01:56]. The posture that follows is simple. Every instruction about volumes, fonts, page counts, submission order, signatures and delivery method is a pass/fail tripwire. Build the machinery to catch each one before any narrative gets written, and treat the matrix as the backbone of the whole response rather than end-of-cycle paperwork.

The second point of agreement is the read. CHCEDC's rule is 'Don't assume anything and understand everything.' Read and reread every attachment. Attend site visits and pre-proposal conferences, because some are mandatory. Ask in writing when one page says 24 and another says 30, and acknowledge every amendment [46vBsddH6zQ @ 00:10:54]. APMP calls this shredding. Read the full RFP without skimming, then pull every shall, must, will and should into a compliance matrix. The matrix then serves as both a map and a review checklist, so nothing slips through the cracks [MSvfidBACFs @ 00:01:16]. Bid and Comply reads the whole pack: ITB, spec, HSE, contract terms and clarifications. It logs one requirement per row in the client's exact words, each with a reference number [c73xWsLDDhc @ 00:01:05]. GovKidMethod shows why the read cannot stop at the summary page. The FBO listing for an Army Corps janitorial job at Bardwell Lake showed no set-aside, which implied full and open competition against large firms. The attached RFP actually declared a 100% small-business set-aside, 'because these guys don't always fill the FBO page out properly' [wot0JsK9qCc @ 00:08:19]. All four voices draw the same lesson: a solicitation is full of traps, and the operator who reads it most slowly and carefully wins on compliance.

Practitioners also agree on timing and on screening the economics. Government Contract Blueprint's first instruction is to build the matrix before writing anything. The matrix stays an internal working tool unless the solicitation requires you to submit it [jSDqXlz5MbI @ 00:00:26]. CHCEDC applies its go/no-go test after checking Section C for scope and clearance requirements and teaming up to fill capability gaps. The test comes down to one question: 'can you make money?' [46vBsddH6zQ @ 00:20:31]. Toledo SBDC is harsher. If you are unsure about profit, 'This should not be your contract.' Know the FAR clauses and never overpromise to an agency to get the award [WqniKXcYJAw @ 00:05:39]. Virtual 24-7 runs a four-question screen: do you meet the requirements, can you handle the size, do you have past experience, and can you compete? It then sets a hard pricing floor: never bid below your true cost. As the speaker puts it, 'If you win a contract you can't afford to do well, it will hurt your reputation and your chances of winning future contracts' [yH2TsdfzuTM @ 00:02:49]. Across these voices, go/no-go is an economic filter first and a writing exercise second. If margin, capability or eligibility is missing, matrix work stops before the narrative starts, and the hours go to the next solicitation.

sections.title: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: The matrix has a set structure. Government Contract Blueprint uses seven columns: reference, requirement, type, proposal section, owner, status and evaluation factor. The evaluation factor column links Section L to Section M. Its sample row logs L 2.3, three past-performance examples, Volume 2 and relevance/quality, with the row owned by business development and its status set to in progress [jSDqXlz5MbI @ 00:03:32]. Bid and Comply adds a flag for mandatory pass/fail versus scored, and a status ladder of not started, in progress, complete and reviewed. In the final pass, an independent checker opens every page reference, and any blank evidence cell counts as a gap [c73xWsLDDhc @ 00:02:42]. Lindauer builds the outline to levels three and four and embeds evaluation adjectives such as 'demonstrated approach' in the headings. She allocates page budget by evaluation weight. In her Defense Health Agency example, Volume 1 was capped at 25 pages, with a 16-page narrative and a 5-page QC plan [zeJUuxLmj6s @ 00:07:09]. CHCEDC's crosswalk heading, '1.5 Transition Plan (C.3, L, M.5)', puts the Section C, L and M references in the title itself. Evaluators can then score each section without hunting for it, because, in the director's words, 'They're scoring it' [46vBsddH6zQ @ 00:33:39].

AI speeds up the shred, but everyone who uses it keeps a human on the final check. The Promptly App puts the manual baseline at four hours minimum with tools, and up to a week on a large RFP. Its workflow runs four prompts. Section L, the evaluation criteria and the SOW pages are extracted as three files. Text is pulled verbatim, with multi-part requirements split into A/B/C. Everything is then merged into a numbered outline workbook that later feeds the red team. The tool costs $9.99/month or $49.99/year [VvYb0nAHXrc @ 00:03:09]. Point2Pivot's DFO workflow loads the 65-page PDF into NotebookLM. That produced an 11-minute audio deep dive and a briefing doc used to check qualification. ChatGPT then built the writing prompt, and the full PDF, not the summary, went into ChatGPT and Claude side by side [LmEpAxUzd94 @ 00:16:35]. The verdict was 'Claude all the way,' because ChatGPT's sections came back 'very light.' Claude still invented a '64+' projects figure and broke the phase timing, jumping from weeks 9-32 to 33-40 [LmEpAxUzd94 @ 00:26:41]. APMP's warning covers the whole stack. Parsing software and AI are fine for complex documents, but 'Automation is no substitute for accuracy' [MSvfidBACFs @ 00:00:59].

Pricing is where the numbers get concrete. Point2Pivot's DFO bid priced the initial period at $1,850 per day for 90 days, roughly $166K. The option period ran $1,925 per day for 30 days, roughly $57K. The all-inclusive total came to about $224K within the NCR, under a 70/30 technical-to-price weighting [LmEpAxUzd94 @ 00:38:35]. GovKidMethod's janitorial breakdown shows the traps buried in a low-barrier bid. Pad pricing for supplies. Build travel into the line items: 'don't expect them to be paying for your travel.' Price in the $125-per-instance deduction for service logged but not performed. Split the seasons, since the site runs 12 restrooms April through September and only 4 in winter; miss that and 'you would quickly over bid this contract' [wot0JsK9qCc @ 00:23:14]. When budgets are unclear, ProcuraFind first checks the FAQs and the question cutoff, then uses price bracketing such as '$50,000-$150,000.' Its number loads in PM, operational, admin, marketing and materials costs [UcFlKExo_dc @ 00:09:52]. For delivery, CHCEDC's rule is to submit early, because 12:01 for a noon deadline is rejected. Uploads should never wait for the final hour before the cutoff on the portal [46vBsddH6zQ @ 00:55:10].

callout.body: Small habits the speakers use to protect compliance and keep their edge through the Q&A and amendment cycle.
items: Questions are taken in writing only and the answers are published in an addendum to every bidder, so never reveal your unique advantage in a question [CHCEDC — 46vBsddH6zQ @ 00:12:11]

Add every clarification to the matrix the day it arrives. If the client supplies its own compliance form, submit that form and keep your detailed matrix internal [Bid and Comply — c73xWsLDDhc @ 00:03:26]

PWS documents often lack page numbers, so key matrix rows to PWS section numbers so writers and reviewers can always find the source requirement [THE FEDERAL PROPOSAL EXPERTS — zeJUuxLmj6s @ 00:08:42]

sop_steps.action: Build the outline to levels 3-4 and allocate pages by evaluation weight.
sop_steps.detail: Paste every relevant requirement into its proposal-section row, then give the page budget to whatever carries the most weight in the evaluation criteria [THE FEDERAL PROPOSAL EXPERTS — zeJUuxLmj6s @ 00:06:34]

sop_steps.title: Final Check and Early Submission
sop_steps.action: Verify every row against the official solicitation, then upload well ahead of the deadline.
sop_steps.detail: Check answers, attachments, signatures and page limits against the matrix, and verify any AI-drafted rows by hand [Government Contract Blueprint — jSDqXlz5MbI @ 00:04:28]

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: Every shop builds a compliance matrix, but they split on the tool used to build it. Keli Krueger-Huhra of CHCEDC builds it as a spreadsheet straight out of FAR 52.212-1, logging checks such as 10-point font and a 10-page maximum row by row [46vBsddH6zQ @ 00:23:38]. Shannon Lindauer of THE FEDERAL PROPOSAL EXPERTS rejects Excel and works in Word because “it’s easier to navigate and cut and paste from the solicitation.” They build the outline down to levels three and four and embed evaluation adjectives like “demonstrated approach” in the headings [zeJUuxLmj6s @ 00:02:40]. Bid and Comply runs a stricter row discipline: one requirement per row, a reference number on each, the client’s exact words, and a mandatory-versus-scored flag. When the client supplies its own compliance form, they fill that form and keep their matrix internal [c73xWsLDDhc @ 00:03:47]. Government Contract Blueprint also keeps the matrix internal unless the solicitation demands submission. It adds an evaluation-factor column that links every Section L instruction to its Section M score [jSDqXlz5MbI @ 00:00:26]. The format is a preference. What none of these shops will skip is tying each requirement to an owner, a status, and the exact place in the proposal that answers it.

The sharpest split is over how much to write. CHCEDC teaches a one-page executive summary that reads standalone, carries no pricing, and gets written last: “So, you’re going to write this at the very end” [46vBsddH6zQ @ 00:47:28]. Lindauer cuts it outright: “If the government hasn’t expressly requested an executive summary, it shouldn’t be in your proposal” [zeJUuxLmj6s @ 00:03:31]. ProcuraFind writes more. It structures every response as Bio, Process, Budget, Differentiators. The bio runs one to two pages with references and testimonials. The process section gives five to seven high-level steps plus three to four case studies in Problem-Solution-Result format [UcFlKExo_dc @ 00:06:29]. GovKidMethod, breaking down an Army Corps janitorial job at Bardwell Lake, reports the opposite end: “the good news is they really don’t want a proposal they just want some information filled out with a price on it.” That job needed only a bid schedule, a contractor info sheet, and a single PDF by email. The low barrier to entry turned it into a pure price fight [wot0JsK9qCc @ 00:12:48]. CHCEDC takes a middle line on RFQs. Explain how you arrived at the price, confirm the delivered price, attach reps and certs, and “don’t do anything more than what they ask.”

Speed claims differ by an order of magnitude. Point2Pivot claims a good government RFP response in “about 15 minutes or less.” They ran a 65-page DFO solicitation through NotebookLM for a briefing doc and an 11-minute podcast, had ChatGPT build the prompt, then ran that prompt in ChatGPT and Claude side by side. ChatGPT 4.0 came back “very light,” and the verdict was “Claude all the way” [LmEpAxUzd94 @ 00:28:47]. The Promptly App sets a far heavier baseline: at least four hours with tools, and up to a week on a large RFP. Its four prompts cut that down. They pull Section L, evaluation criteria, and SOW text verbatim, split multi-part requirements into A/B/C, and merge everything into a numbered outline workbook. A human approves every file [VvYb0nAHXrc @ 00:03:24]. Lindauer, working manually in Word, budgets four to ten hours for the matrix alone [zeJUuxLmj6s @ 00:12:43]. APMP is the most skeptical of automation. Parsing software or AI is acceptable for complex documents, but “automation is no substitute for accuracy,” and the output must be verified before it feeds the compliance map [MSvfidBACFs @ 00:00:59]. Nobody here argues against using AI. The disagreement is over how much human verification time to budget on top of it.

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most common way to lose is administrative, not technical. Shannon Lindauer of THE FEDERAL PROPOSAL EXPERTS reports that many offerors are eliminated at the contracting officer’s first review for font, outline, or missing-content non-compliance. That is why they build the matrix before the kickoff meeting, and why their shop claims 100% compliant submissions [zeJUuxLmj6s @ 00:01:03]. CHCEDC focuses on the clock and the rules. A 12:01 upload against a noon deadline is rejected. Proposing exceptions to Section L can make the bid non-responsive. As they put it, “in a bid, responsiveness is unforgiving” [46vBsddH6zQ @ 00:58:15]. Bid and Comply opens with “Most tenders are not lost on price” and names three repeat mistakes. Teams build the matrix late, write “noted/complied” with no evidence behind the claim, and ignore clarifications instead of logging each one the day it arrives [c73xWsLDDhc @ 00:03:04]. The IDC Tirisano team adds a portal trap: there is no submit button. Whatever sits in the folder at 5:00 is the submission. Usi Pilo asked applicants not to start the workbook on 5 November for a 6 November close [Sh4XERIYcuY @ 01:00:10]. Every one of these losses happens before an evaluator reads a single technical strength.

Pricing traps are where operators lose money after winning. GovKidMethod flags the seasonality clause in the Bardwell Lake job: 12 restrooms serviced April through September, but only 4 in winter. As they warn, “if you didn’t catch this you would quickly over bid this contract and try and like bid out the whole year.” The same job carries a $125 deduction per instance where service is logged but not performed. Travel must be built into the line items, and supply costs should be padded [wot0JsK9qCc @ 00:24:01]. Virtual 24-7 sets the price floor at true cost, because “if you win a contract you can’t afford to do well, it will hurt your reputation and your chances of winning future contracts” [yH2TsdfzuTM @ 00:02:49]. Toledo Small Business Development Center is blunter: if you are unsure whether you will make a profit, “this should not be your contract” [WqniKXcYJAw @ 00:05:39]. Presales Talk shows how an unclarified spec can blow up a budget. With no RPO or RTO stated, 800 replication licenses could eat 50 Cr of a 100 Cr budget. A missing five-year growth plan on 300TB creates penalty and legal exposure. Their margin rule is that “no company work on a bid for negative margin.” Keep a negotiation buffer, and never reveal the margin [V5HydwGhK8o @ 01:25:20].

The third failure class is trusting the document, or the machine, too much. GovKidMethod read an FBO summary page that showed no set-aside, which implied full and open competition against large firms. The attached RFP declared a 100% small-business set-aside instead: “this is why you got a check because these guys don’t always fill the FBO page out properly” [wot0JsK9qCc @ 00:08:19]. Presales Talk says every RFP needs discovery because in “99% cases” the information is not clear, and warns “So don’t assume that RFP is right.” Their revised-RFP example changed 10 switches to 15 in the middle of a bid [V5HydwGhK8o @ 00:14:36]. Point2Pivot caught Claude inventing “64+” complex system transformation projects: “I suspect it kind of made that up.” The same draft had phase timing that jumped from weeks 9–32 to 33–40. The practitioner said they would keep the 64+ figure as a “psychological marker” only if it proved true [LmEpAxUzd94 @ 00:26:41]. The IDC Tirisano team flags a date trap. The submission deadline moved, but document validity is still judged against 19 October, so applicants must not edit the workbook dates. Using AI to break the workbook’s protection will also be caught, because the workbook will be audited [Sh4XERIYcuY @ 00:16:08].

callout.title: Four Kill Checks Before You Submit
callout.body: Each check below comes from a loss or near-miss practitioners reported. Clear all four before the bid leaves your hands.
items: Confirm the NAICS code on the solicitation is on your SAM registration, because the award cannot be made without it [GovKidMethod — wot0JsK9qCc @ 00:02:06].
Have an independent checker open every page reference in the matrix, because a blank evidence cell is a gap [Bid and Comply — c73xWsLDDhc @ 00:02:42].
Walk away if you are unsure the job turns a profit, because if profit is in doubt, this should not be your contract [Toledo Small Business Development Center — WqniKXcYJAw @ 00:05:39].
Take scope interpretations only from the warranted contracting officer, because the COR cannot change the contract [GovKidMethod — wot0JsK9qCc @ 00:05:54].

chapters.pull_quote: “So, just keep in mind that in a bid, responsiveness is unforgiving.” — CHCEDC (46vBsddH6zQ @ 00:58:15).
action_checklist: Before kickoff, shred the full solicitation and every attachment into a matrix with one requirement per row. Use the client's exact words and flag must, shall, will, and required [Bid and Comply — c73xWsLDDhc @ 00:01:05].
Redline every amendment into the matrix and note which amendment it is current through, such as up-to-date through amendment 002 [THE FEDERAL PROPOSAL EXPERTS — zeJUuxLmj6s @ 00:12:04].
Before the go/no-go call, cross-check the summary page against the attached RFP for set-aside, NAICS, and place of performance [GovKidMethod — wot0JsK9qCc @ 00:08:19].
Price seasons, travel, and per-instance deductions as separate line items so you never overbid the full year [GovKidMethod — wot0JsK9qCc @ 00:23:14].
Run AI drafts side by side, then strip any invented figures and recheck phase timing by hand before submission [Point2Pivot — LmEpAxUzd94 @ 00:26:41].
Request a debriefing in writing within 3 days, even if you win [Toledo Small Business Development Center — WqniKXcYJAw @ 00:08:31].

chapters.question_prompt: How do I find primes and subcontractors, and how should teaming agreements be structured so I don't get burned?
chapters.title: Teaming, Subcontracting and Prime–Sub Relationships
chapters.subtitle: Prime vs. sub paths for beginners, finding primes (SAIC) and handling ghosting subs, teaming agreements vs. subcontracts vs. JVs, negotiating from the sub's side, the financial trade-offs between prime and sub, and VA OSDBU and PCI teaming guidance
chapters.executive_summary: Sixteen GovCon practitioners converge on one rule: the prime is whoever the contracting officer signs with, it carries full liability, and subs only get paid what is locked in writing. Operators report teaming lifts win probability when it fills a named gap, while handshake deals end in ghosting, six-month removals and a $20,000 loss. Street mechanics include pulling price history from FPDS, mining SAM.gov contract awards (2,000 help-desk hits filtered to 87 woman-owned targets), setting 51-52% prime workshare, enforcing the 50% services limitation on subcontracting, and funding roughly 14% of contract value upfront as prime versus 20% as sub. Practitioners split on whether rushing to team helps or damages small firms, how much exclusivity matters, and whether written teaming agreements are actually enforceable in court.

sections.heading: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every practitioner starts from the same hard line: the prime is the company the contracting officer signed with, and that is where all liability sits. ASI Education explains that the prime holds privity of contract, the government has no privity with subs, and FAR Part 44 bars the agency from dictating which subs a prime uses; even a multi-company team still has one accountable 'belly button' [jYYGaPkanFU @ 00:01:41]. Shane, the legal voice on the VA OSDBU panel, puts it bluntly: the prime is 100% responsible to the government, including when a sub goes bankrupt or trips Service Contract Act problems [iLuva0z2cMA @ 00:57:00]. Federal Contracts Lab frames prime and sub as responsibility levels rather than status levels. The prime signs, manages, invoices and eats the performance risk, while subs plug in as HVAC, janitorial, pest control, help desk or cyber specialists [3eoJWm0WffU @ 00:03:19]. Neil McDonnell attacks the assumption that 'prime' means 'large': a small service-disabled veteran-owned business won a $175M prime with Booz Allen and Boeing working underneath it, and an aircraft carrier runs on roughly a thousand subs [zqg5q_pZvdc @ 00:07:38]. The operating takeaway is simple: whoever signs owns the risk, and everyone else at the table is negotiating for a protected slice.

The second point of near-total agreement: if it is not written, it does not exist. Stephanie of GovCon TechLab opens with the classic burn, a handshake teaming deal where the sub does 80% of the work for 20% of the revenue or gets ghosted after the partner wins, and dismisses a one-page letter of intent as a 'hope document,' because after award the prime holds all the leverage [JYbjE63rG-Y @ 00:04:26]. Dr. Mel lists exactly what happens without a real teaming agreement: lost control of IP, exclusion from the final deal, ownership disputes and proposal hours that never pay back, then tells operators to stop running on 'handshakes and hope' [HKtAZzSL_GQ @ 00:01:23]. The VA OSDBU panel warns that any prime offering 49% of a project but refusing to put it in writing deserves extreme caution [iLuva0z2cMA @ 00:26:33]. Centurion Research Solutions sharpens the drafting standard: the work percentage should name a specific percentage or number of staff, because agreements that promise 'best efforts' or 'goals' rarely pan out [L-BpgTTiESM @ 00:10:18]. Across all four practitioners, the rule is identical: lock precise numbers on paper before the proposal ships, never vague percentages, verbal assurances or friendly intentions.

Practitioners also agree that subcontracting is a legitimate entry and growth lane, not a consolation prize. Humam Finding Sam points out that the FAR mandates primes subcontract set percentages to small businesses, so prime compliance goals create built-in demand, and a firm with zero government past performance can get its foot in the door this way, adding that primes need subs as much as subs need primes [T_HZxPdh7B8 @ 00:00:25]. Federal Contracts Lab states flatly that subcontracting is not a downgrade, pitching a hybrid of subcontracting plus selective small primes in the same service and buyer type, and telling subs to document every engagement for references [3eoJWm0WffU @ 00:08:57]. Akiesha Foster, who won as key personnel in a tier-two sub slot, says teammates are typically considered six to twelve months before the request for proposal is released, so operators should stop waiting until the last minute and start building relationships now [qnkHiXcQCHM @ 00:05:18]. ELINT Capital's panel adds the money logic: subcontracting beats getting nothing, but the single most important move is picking the prime carefully and keeping a good relationship with it [EpUc9OVjb4g @ 00:18:07]. The shared sequence across all four is sub first, collect documented proof, then prime selectively when ready.
