sections.heading: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: The prospecting mechanics are concrete. Neil McDonnell's SAM.gov workflow: log in, go to Search, then Contracting, then Contract Awards, and search the exact phrase 'help desk' for about 2,000 results; filter to woman-owned small businesses, certified or not, to get 149; download and strip duplicates by awardee UEI, which removed 62 and left 87 companies to approach [zqg5q_pZvdc @ 00:20:35]. He favors firms with $20 million and above in awards and says the point is future relationships, not asking for a cut of existing contracts. Akiesha Foster Googles the top 100 federal contractors, builds a spreadsheet, uses usaspending.gov to pick a target like SAIC, then maps its small business program, specialist contact, supplier portal and teaming process [qnkHiXcQCHM @ 00:00:45]. Humam Finding Sam runs the channel's own SAM Search tool with subcontracting-source filters on names like Lockheed Martin or Deloitte, using a 'high' confidence filter to surface FAR-required subcontracts, plus plain-English queries and weekly saved-search alerts [T_HZxPdh7B8 @ 00:03:53]. Kizzy Parks works the other direction as prime: call vendors the moment an opportunity posts, before they are exhausted by the 107th caller, and find who won similar work in the same location, then ask who they subbed to, such as a gravel supplier [F6Hwh89ornQ @ 00:08:58].

Workshare math is where deals live or die. On the VA OSDBU panel, Shane lays out the limitation on subcontracting: services 50%, general construction 15% with 85% to subs, specialty trade 25% with 75% to subs, measured separately for each base and option period with no averaging; on a $1M woman-owned set-aside with $100k of airfare excluded, the prime must perform $450k of the remaining $900k, and a similarly situated sub's $200k stacks with the prime's $300k to reach $500k [iLuva0z2cMA @ 01:10:26]. Jackie Lopez on the same panel sets a 51-52% floor whenever socioeconomics are involved. Theodore Watson says the prime generally performs at least 51% of contract cost, less depending on the industry code, and that 31% of companies using teaming agreements or JVs are not familiar with the landmines competitors use in bid protests [NP_UB6qiZhw @ 00:00:31]. Stephanie at GovCon TechLab turns this into a filter: a prime promising 60% of the work on a services set-aside is offering a deal that is illegal on its face [JYbjE63rG-Y @ 00:12:50]. The Centurion Research Solutions session confirms small-business primes usually retain 51% of revenue [L-BpgTTiESM @ 00:04:04]. The operator rule: run the dollar math per period before signing anything, because the limitation can cost the award itself.

The money mechanics are just as specific. ELINT Capital's worked example: a $2M-per-year services task order on a set-aside, with the prime doing 55%, burns about $80k a month and waits 70-80 days for payment; with a roughly $175k payroll reserve, total upfront hits $275-300k, about 14% of contract value, while a sub holding a $400k slice needs about $80k upfront, about 20% [EpUc9OVjb4g @ 00:13:32]. The same panel says subs now push pay-when-paid clauses capped at about 60 days, because an improper invoice restarts the 30-day clock, and should fund 2-2.5 months of payroll. On pricing, Kizzy Parks tells primes to ask the agency what it paid before and to check fpds.gov, warning that taking a sub quote and simply tacking a profit percentage on top is not going to happen [F6Hwh89ornQ @ 00:04:37]. Jackie Lopez builds price to win from FPDS or a Googled contract number, adjusted for changes, noting most bidders come in 5-10% under, and insists price to win and price to execute must be one and the same [iLuva0z2cMA @ 01:26:27]. ASI Education describes the squeeze in sole-source negotiations: either the prime tells the contracting officer the sub cannot go any cheaper, or everyone cuts about 10% [jYYGaPkanFU @ 00:07:17].

callout.title: Moves the operators actually run
callout.body: Small clause choices and vetting habits that practitioners say decide whether a teaming slot turns into paid work.
items: Make exclusivity task-order-level, not IDIQ-level, and make sure exclusivity does not survive termination while confidentiality and employee non-solicitation do [Streamline Government Contracts, LLC — W-f5dCQEEkE @ 00:09:32].
Get sub pricing in writing even by text or WhatsApp; one winner had to give a contract back because the sub contact had left the company [Kizzy Parks — F6Hwh89ornQ @ 00:07:00].

Vet a partner's core values by checking the CEO's LinkedIn connections and calling trusted mutual contacts, then run FPDS EZ Search, USAspending, SBA Dynamic Small Business Search and SAM.gov [VA OSDBU (On Demand) — iLuva0z2cMA @ 00:24:25].
Pull a D&B report on any small prime before signing; one prime on a team was declared financially unacceptable [Centurion Research Solutions — L-BpgTTiESM @ 00:10:56].

sop_steps.title: Build the target list
sop_steps.action: Mine SAM.gov Contract Awards for your exact service phrase, filter by socioeconomic status, and deduplicate by UEI.
sop_steps.detail: Search the exact phrase, filter to the set-aside category, download, remove duplicates by awardee UEI, and prioritize firms with $20 million and above in awards [Neil McDonnell — zqg5q_pZvdc @ 00:24:05].

sop_steps.title: Name the gap and assess the partner
sop_steps.action: Answer the four Assess questions before any outreach or signature.
sop_steps.detail: Confirm what gap teaming fixes, reject duplicate capabilities like two WOSB cyber firms, check the workshare math, and verify the partner pays through references, factoring companies and protests [GovCon TechLab — JYbjE63rG-Y @ 00:11:24].

sop_steps.title: Paper the deal before submission
sop_steps.action: Sign the NDA first, then the teaming agreement before the proposal goes in, using attorney-drafted templates.
sop_steps.detail: Sign an NDA before disclosing relationships and sign the teaming agreement before submission, with a 51-52% prime floor when socioeconomics are involved [VA OSDBU (On Demand) — iLuva0z2cMA @ 00:43:38].

sop_steps.title: Track the relationship post-award
sop_steps.action: Run a fixed cadence of check-ins and invoice reviews and put every rate change in writing.
sop_steps.detail: Hold weekly 15-minute check-ins, monthly invoice reviews and quarterly relationship reviews; on a FEMA option period, reduced rates were passed through to the sub in writing [GovCon TechLab — JYbjE63rG-Y @ 00:19:53].

sections.heading: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: Kizzy Parks breaks hardest from the teaming chorus. She says SBA, SCORE and similar outfits push the line that “government loves teams,” and she calls rushing to team “one of the most damaging” practices; her rule is to define the goal first, whether that is higher win odds, fatter margins, or a new client type, and then ask why a stronger party needs you at all [ol1KkwjDTqg @ 00:00:45]. Jackie Lopez reads the same market the opposite way, crediting teaming principles with having “significantly increased our Revenue” and pinning 50–60% of her growth on a reputation as a good teaming partner [iLuva0z2cMA @ 00:14:52]. Stephanie of GovCon TechLab lands between them with a one-line filter: “If you can't name the specific gap that you're trying to fill, then you don't really need to team,” and two WOSB cyber firms pairing up is a “hard pass” [JYbjE63rG-Y @ 00:12:00]. Mike Lore adds the relationship trap, warning operators to “avoid teaming just because it's somebody you already know” and to “team to win,” setting selection criteria before picking anyone [L-BpgTTiESM @ 00:08:57]. The practical split: Lopez teams early and often to lift P-win, while Parks teams only when her chips are on the table.

The sequencing fight is just as sharp. Kizzy Parks teaches middleman priming from day one: you win as prime, others deliver the service or product, and she closes by saying you need no past performance and no product to play [F6Hwh89ornQ @ 00:11:55]. Akiesha Foster runs the opposite clock, holding Level 3 certification and 12+ years of experience yet planning about 10 years as a tier-two sub before priming, because “start off as a subcontractor and then that will position you better so you can become a prime” [qnkHiXcQCHM @ 00:07:08]. Neil McDonnell rejects the ladder framing altogether, arguing subcontracting is not just for small or new firms and pushing three revenue streams in parallel: subbing under a small, priming, and subbing under a large, with all three in play once traction passes $3M [zqg5q_pZvdc @ 00:11:06]. Federal Contracts Lab treats prime and sub as responsibility levels rather than status, insists “Subcontracting is not a downgrade,” and prescribes a hybrid of subcontracting plus selective small primes in the same service and buyer type, summed up as “It's about sequence” [3eoJWm0WffU @ 00:14:25]. Foster's timing warning compounds the choice: teammates are typically picked six to 12 months before the RFP, so “don't wait to the last minute.”

Paperwork depth splits the field. Parks tells middleman primes no exclusive agreement or NDA is needed with vendors, only “some type of written paper trail of pricing,” even by text or WhatsApp [F6Hwh89ornQ @ 00:07:00]. Stephanie demands the full seven-clause stack, including a mutual NDA, proposal-cost terms, termination if not awarded, a workshare floor where “no less than 30%” beats “approximately,” and mutual exclusivity per opportunity only, never blanket [JYbjE63rG-Y @ 00:14:55]. David Gallagher of Kutak Rock tempers both camps on enforceability: “The agreement to agree interpretation of a teaming agreement is by far the most common,” the enforceable EG&G v. Cube outcome “is rare,” and “Exclusivity is not critical, but it helps” [NB57wtT4xfs @ 00:48:53]. Karen Long, negotiating from the sub's seat, wants exclusivity at the task-order level rather than the IDIQ level and no unilateral right for the prime to drop you, warning that “if you're going to be exclusive you should understand what you are giving up” [W-f5dCQEEkE @ 00:09:32]. Gallagher's own baseline is blunt: “Never sign just a standard teaming agreement,” because no standard federal or DOD form exists, so you start from a template and tailor it.

sections.heading: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The costliest losses came from deals that lived on trust. Jackie Lopez was pushed off a five-year contract within six months by a greed-driven prime, and her lawsuit recovered only part of the first year's profit; and her warning is blunt: “if someone tells you that they're going to give you 49 of a project but they're not willing to put it in writing I would be very careful about that” [iLuva0z2cMA @ 00:25:31]. Kizzy Parks took a man's promise of a monthly “bonus” for access to her existing client, collected 1 of 12 payments, had no signed agreement, and ate roughly $20,000 [ol1KkwjDTqg @ 00:06:22]. Mike Lore watched his team get “awarded eight of these 11 but my company only received actual work on two,” and he warns: “avoid agreements that promise best efforts or goals these rarely pan out,” calling a poor teaming agreement “a shotgun wedding” [L-BpgTTiESM @ 00:12:41]. Stephanie's warning covers the same ground: a one-page letter of intent is a “hope document,” after award the prime holds all the leverage, and a handshake deal is how you end up “doing 80% of the work and getting only 20% of the revenue” [JYbjE63rG-Y @ 00:03:34].

ELINT Capital says prime-or-sub is often dictated by capital, credit line and cash position. Its worked example on a $2M-per-year set-aside services task order has the prime doing 55% at roughly $80k a month, waiting 70–80 days for payment, holding a payroll reserve near $175k, and fronting $275–300k, about 14% of contract value, while a sub with a $400k slice needs about $80k up front, about 20% [EpUc9OVjb4g @ 00:13:32]. The same panel flags subs pushing pay-when-paid clauses capped near 60 days, improper invoices restarting the 30-day clock, DOGE freezes holding payments 3–4 months, and near-annual shutdowns; its advice is to fund 2–2.5 months of payroll, and “it's better to subcontract than to get nothing” [EpUc9OVjb4g @ 00:18:29]. Jackie Lopez prices the bid side of the burn: a 30k proposal cost across 10 proposals is 300k spent with nothing won [iLuva0z2cMA @ 00:14:31]. ASI Education lived the LPTA version: as a sub it refused to drop lower and lost, then watched the winner post low DC salaries on LinkedIn; it calls LPTA “a race to the bottom” where lowballers try to get “made well” through modifications [jYYGaPkanFU @ 00:23:25]. Kizzy Parks adds the margin trap: taking a vendor quote and simply bolting on a profit percentage, “it's not going to happen” [F6Hwh89ornQ @ 00:04:57].

Compliance landmines turn wins into forfeits. Theodore Watson says 31% of firms using teaming agreements or JVs are “not quite familiar” with the landmines competitors use to get an award revoked in a bid protest, starting with limitations on subcontracting, where the prime generally performs at least 51% of contract cost, and affiliation when a partner “exercises too much control over the contract” [NP_UB6qiZhw @ 00:00:14]. Stephanie makes it concrete: “if a prime is promising you 60% of the work on a service contract set-aside, that deal is illegal on its face” [JYbjE63rG-Y @ 00:12:50]. VA OSDBU's Shane adds that limitation-on-subcontracting compliance is measured per base and option period with no averaging, and the prime stays 100% responsible to the government, including for sub bankruptcy and Service Contract Act issues [iLuva0z2cMA @ 01:03:40]. On partner vetting, Mike Lore pulls a D&B report on small primes, cites one prime that was declared financially unacceptable, vets the prime's proposal capability, asks the client's view of partners, verifies citations, and makes contingent hires [L-BpgTTiESM @ 00:11:13]. His exit rule for stalling partners: “in the case of reluctant suitors the sooner you walk away the better.”

callout.title: Four checks before you sign onto any team
callout.body: Every gate below comes from a loss, lockout or forfeit a named practitioner reported. Clear all four before the proposal goes in.
items: Workshare is written as a floor, not a hope: “no less than 30%” beats “approximately,” and a 49% promise nobody will put in writing is a red flag [GovCon TechLab — JYbjE63rG-Y @ 00:14:55].

Duration and survival are nailed down: the agreement has an end date, exclusivity does not survive, and it cannot terminate while the proposal is in source selection [Streamline Government Contracts, LLC — W-f5dCQEEkE @ 00:18:33].

Limitation-on-subcontracting math is run per period: services 50%, general construction 15%/85%, specialty trade 25%/75%, measured per base and option period with no averaging [VA OSDBU (On Demand) — iLuva0z2cMA @ 01:09:29].
Cash runway covers the payment lag: fund 2–2.5 months of payroll and consider invoice insurance when the prime is unfamiliar [ELINT Capital — EpUc9OVjb4g @ 00:53:13].

chapters.pull_quote: “A handshake teaming deal is how you end up doing 80% of the work and getting only 20% of the revenue or even worse being ghosted when you found out your teaming partner has won a contract.” — GovCon TechLab (JYbjE63rG-Y @ 00:00:00).
action_checklist: Name the specific capability gap a partner fills before you team, and pass on partners who duplicate what you already have [GovCon TechLab — JYbjE63rG-Y @ 00:12:00].

Vet a partner's core values by checking the CEO's LinkedIn connections and calling trusted mutual contacts, then pull award history from FPDS, USAspending, SBA Dynamic Small Business Search and SAM.gov [VA OSDBU (On Demand) — iLuva0z2cMA @ 00:24:25].
Pull a D&B report on any small prime, vet its proposal capability, and discuss pricing up front before committing [Centurion Research Solutions — L-BpgTTiESM @ 00:10:56].

Write workshare “for the duration of the contract including all option periods” and add a pricing-lock clause so accepted pricing carries into the subcontract [Streamline Government Contracts, LLC — W-f5dCQEEkE @ 00:06:00].
Run the limitation-on-subcontracting math on real numbers: a $1M WOSB contract minus $100k airfare leaves $900k, so the prime must perform $450k [VA OSDBU (On Demand) — iLuva0z2cMA @ 01:10:26].
Model the cash before choosing prime or sub, and fund 2–2.5 months of payroll to survive payment lags [ELINT Capital — EpUc9OVjb4g @ 00:53:13].

chapters.question_prompt: How much work must I perform myself, and what compliance and fraud risks come with passing work through?
chapters.title: Limitations on Subcontracting, Affiliation and Enforcement
chapters.subtitle: 13 CFR 125.6 and the 50% rule, SBA's updated rules, similarly situated entities, ostensible contractor and affiliation risk, FAR Part 44 and flow-down compliance for subs, and DOJ fraud prosecutions such as Operation Ghostbusters
chapters.executive_summary: Federal set-aside primes agree on one hard rule: the small business that wins the award must keep a fixed share of the dollars, measured as amount paid to non-similarly-situated subs. Services and supplies cap subcontracted pay at 50%, general construction at 85%, and specialty trades at 75%, with materials excluded. Similarly situated entities, first-tier subs holding the prime's status and small under the subcontract NAICS, count as the prime's own work, and PilieroMazza says a WOSB can push 100% to a WOSB SSE. Compliance is measured per base or option period or task order, tracked monthly, and enforced through negative CPARS, debarment and rising DOJ probes. Practitioners split on whether construction self-performance is 15% or 25%, which NAICS governs SSE size, and whether leasing a sub's employees is a legitimate workaround.

sections.heading: 1. The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every practitioner starts from the same premise: the limitation on subcontracting is a performance rule that binds the small business that won a set-aside, not the subs and not full-and-open winners. GovPrep tells primes to pull up SF 1449 and read Block 10 before assuming the clause is live, walking through a 2013 set-aside under NAICS 311422 as the example [bg9NY9VUfsE @ 00:00:41]. PilieroMazza widens the net: the limit attaches to all set-asides, and the only carve-out is a small business set-aside below the simplified acquisition threshold [i9prjadeAyM @ 00:10:51]. The measuring stick has also changed. PilieroMazza traces the 2016 overhaul that moved the calculation from personnel cost to amount paid [qxE-37z0qfw @ 00:06:28], and the SDVOSB prime behind Vet GovCon Blueprint compresses the point into two words, dollars paid, rejecting hours or headcount as the yardstick [go1eoNNgFRM @ 00:01:34]. Under that standard, the number that matters is what gets paid to each non-similarly-situated sub against the total paid on the contract. The baseline sequence the speakers share is to confirm set-aside status in the award document, identify the governing clause, which GovPrep pins to 52.219-14, and build the subcontract budget around dollars before any teaming agreement gets signed.

The percentage ladder is where the speakers line up most tightly. Mark Ryan lays it out cleanly: services at 50%, construction at 85%, specialty trades such as plumbing and electrical at 75%, and manufacturers at 50%, with resellers required to buy from a small domestic manufacturer [ne7XpEiLNKE @ 00:01:06]. PilieroMazza gives the identical ladder for services, manufacturing, general construction and specialty trade, adding that materials come out of the math where applicable [i9prjadeAyM @ 00:14:21]. The Vet GovCon Blueprint operator frames the same numbers as caps on pay to subs that are not similarly situated, excluding materials on supplies, general construction and special trades, and measures mixed contracts portion by portion [go1eoNNgFRM @ 00:01:59]. Theodore Watson adds the warning that not every NAICS runs on a 51/49 split, flagging the 236 and 237 construction series at 15% prime and 85% subs, a figure he prefaces with 'I believe' [28K_7987r8w @ 00:01:19]. Watson also confirms that under a 51/49 split the prime's 51% can be a blend of its own work and similarly situated sub work. For an operator, the takeaway is simple: identify the contract type first, because the allowable subcontract share swings from half the dollars to 85% depending on whether the work is services, supply, general construction or a specialty trade.

The similarly situated entity is the consensus pressure valve. PilieroMazza defines it in three parts: a first-tier sub, holding the same status that qualified the prime, and small under the NAICS code assigned to the subcontract [i9prjadeAyM @ 00:07:08]. Theodore Watson hammers the last prong, saying most people miss that the size test runs on the subcontract NAICS the prime assigns, not the prime's own code [28K_7987r8w @ 00:04:26]. Status must match pairwise, as Watson lists it: small business to small business, 8(a) to 8(a), HUBZone, SDVOSB and WOSB. When it does, the SSE's dollars count as the prime's own performance, which Watson says actually helps the prime. The consensus limit on that valve is that it does not survive a second hop. The Vet GovCon Blueprint operator warns that work an SSE passes downstream counts against the prime [go1eoNNgFRM @ 00:03:54], echoing Watson's rule that anyone other than prime employees or first-tier SSE employees counts against the prime. Enforcement has teeth on the agency side as well. Mark Ryan reports that contracting officers are now required to issue a negative CPARS when a prime misses the requirement [ne7XpEiLNKE @ 00:04:54]. PilieroMazza stacks suspension, debarment and fines on top, and flags DOJ investigations as a rising trend.

sections.heading: 2. Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: The arithmetic is where operators either stay clean or quietly drift out of compliance. PilieroMazza's worked example runs a $1M-per-month services contract carrying $100K in materials: strip the materials, take half of the remaining $900K, and the prime owes $450K of self-performance every month [i9prjadeAyM @ 00:32:49]. The same firm's earlier session clarifies what can be stripped on services work: G&A and overhead stay in the base, while materials that are separately line-itemed can be deducted, illustrated with a janitorial contract [qxE-37z0qfw @ 00:54:18]. Mark Ryan shows the SSE lever in dollars: on a $100K 8(a) IT contract, $20K subbed to another 8(a) still counts toward the prime's $50K [ne7XpEiLNKE @ 00:02:25]. The Vet GovCon Blueprint operator runs the failure case on the same $100K services contract, where at most $50K can flow to subs that are not similarly situated, so a $70K check to one such sub breaks the rule outright [go1eoNNgFRM @ 00:02:38]. GovPrep adds that the services figure is calculated fully burdened with fee. The operating move is a monthly tracking sheet that subtracts eligible materials first, applies the cap to what remains, and then credits only first-tier SSE dollars back to the prime's side of the ledger.

Timing is the second mechanic, and the speakers agree the old back-loaded self-performance play is dead. Mark Ryan says he has watched firms sub 70% in year one, 40% in year two and 10% in year three, then self-perform in year four and get away with it; the updated rule measures compliance per contract year, and on IDIQs per task order, specifically to make audits easier [ne7XpEiLNKE @ 00:03:26]. PilieroMazza calls the belief that a firm can fall short early and make it up over the remaining option years the most common misconception about the rule, because compliance is measured per base or option period [i9prjadeAyM @ 00:38:18]. That pushes tracking cadence to the front of the playbook. PilieroMazza wants the numbers pulled monthly and no less than quarterly [i9prjadeAyM @ 00:43:56], and the Vet GovCon Blueprint operator names silent drift over time as one of three traps, prescribing the same fix of tracking dollars to each sub every month [go1eoNNgFRM @ 00:04:20]. PilieroMazza's earlier session adds that on full-and-open vehicles, the measurement runs per order rather than over the whole vehicle. For a broker structuring a multi-year deal, the build is a running monthly ledger per period and per order, so the prime sees a breach coming before the period closes rather than after.

Paper is the third mechanic. PilieroMazza says a prime may rely on a sub's SAM representations or written representations as of the date of the subcontract offer, with the caveats that HUBZone status must be confirmed against SBA certification and WOSB remains self-certified for subcontracts [i9prjadeAyM @ 00:22:14]. The same firm wants a clause forcing prompt notice of any status change plus indemnification, and its earlier session lists the teaming agreement terms to lock down: NAICS assignment for the sub, size and status representations, and a limitations on subcontracting awareness clause [qxE-37z0qfw @ 00:30:19]. Theodore Watson goes further on the back end, suggesting primes make subs certify compliance with each invoice; he concedes no case law backs it, but says it may help against False Claims and pass-through scrutiny [28K_7987r8w @ 00:08:07]. On the front end, Watson's affiliation session advises spelling out in the proposal itself what percentage of the statement of work the prime will perform versus the sub or teaming partner [k1ZkyITmwWM @ 00:12:00]. PilieroMazza also points to other direct cost exclusions recognized through VA, GSA and DOE class deviations, including airline travel, environmental remediation, cloud computing and mass media, though the Vet GovCon Blueprint operator stresses such exclusions only apply as the solicitation allows.

callout.title: Field Moves for Holding the Prime Share
callout.body: Four moves the speakers teach for keeping the self-performance share defensible and the subcontract paper clean.
items: Verify you actually have the staff and infrastructure before bidding, or be prepared to withdraw the bid [PilieroMazza PLLC — i9prjadeAyM @ 00:04:28].

Bring the December 2018 class deviation 0003 to the table on SSE pooling, because in Eric Coffie's experience contracting officers have asked him to explain the rule [Eric Coffie — 8-4Lml2bZj4 @ 00:01:25].

After selecting a sub, Natalie Rosario asks it to lease one to two of its employees for the duration, providing only what the contract requires with no handbooks or perks; she says hungry subs usually agree [Natalie Rosario | GovCon Coach — G44VRBscagY @ 00:02:31].
Avoid hiring an incumbent's workforce en masse, especially its managers, and never rely on a large sub to manage the contract [Theodore Watson — k1ZkyITmwWM @ 00:10:42].

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split is over which NAICS code decides whether a sub counts as similarly situated. Natalie Rosario of GovCon Coach tells primes to prove the sub's matching status in SAM and says that registration sits 'under the NAICS code of the contract that was awarded' [G44VRBscagY @ 00:01:00]. Theodore Watson contradicts that directly: the sub must be small under the NAICS the prime assigns to the subcontract, not the prime's own code, and Watson warns that 'most people miss this' [28K_7987r8w @ 00:04:26]. PilieroMazza sides with Watson and adds that the subcontract NAICS may carry a higher size standard than the prime's [i9prjadeAyM @ 00:08:35]. The construction numbers fracture the same way. Watson puts general construction at 15% prime and 85% subs, hedged with 'I believe,' and PilieroMazza states 85% for general construction and 75% for specialty trades. Eric Coffie instead describes a '25% requirement' on construction, so that 75% can be subbed [8-4Lml2bZj4 @ 00:03:58], while GovPrep separately states specialty trade as '25.' An operator pricing a construction bid off the wrong speaker builds the self-performance budget on a misstatement, and GovPrep's own answer is to pull the clause, 52.219-14, and check Block 10 of the SF 1449 to confirm the set-aside before committing a number.

How a prime manufactures its self-performance share is the second fault line. Rosario's street play is to select the sub, then ask to 'lease one to two of your employees for the duration'; Rosario reports that hungry subs usually agree and gives those leased workers only what the contract requires, with no handbooks or perks [G44VRBscagY @ 00:02:31]. The counter-pressure comes from how other speakers define the prime's own labor. GovPrep insists the work be done with 'your w-2 employees,' not 1099s and not subcontractors, and PilieroMazza likewise treats independent contractors as subcontractors rather than employees [i9prjadeAyM @ 00:11:35]. Watson attacks the adjacent move of absorbing someone else's people: on affiliation, Watson tells primes to avoid hiring an incumbent's workforce en masse, especially its managers, and not to rely on a large sub to manage the contract [k1ZkyITmwWM @ 00:10:42]. Rosario and Watson do converge on management. Rosario says management and admin do not count toward the prime's 51% of labor, and Watson warns that mere supervision may itself violate the ostensible subcontractor rule because the prime must perform the primary and vital parts [28K_7987r8w @ 00:09:51]. Rosario pairs the leasing play with a hard warning: primes submit yearly prime-versus-sub labor hours and must keep them accurate.

The third split is whether the similarly situated structure is a loophole to exploit or a trap. PilieroMazza walks through a WOSB prime subbing 100% to a WOSB similarly situated entity and concedes 'it's not in violation of the statute or the regulation so sba recognizes the loophole and we'll see' [qxE-37z0qfw @ 00:15:05]; the firm adds that only the CO, the prime or SBA can protest a sub's size. Eric Coffie frames the same rule as help for small firms, describing December 2018 class deviation '0003' letting firms pool similarly situated entities across matching statuses such as HUBZone with HUBZone [8-4Lml2bZj4 @ 00:02:32]. Vet GovCon Blueprint, speaking as an SDVOSB prime, takes the opposite view of pass-through arrangements: 'That's not a loophole — that's the exact scheme this rule was written to stop' [go1eoNNgFRM @ 00:04:42]. Watson lands on the enforcement side, warning that pass-throughs can bring criminal violations [28K_7987r8w @ 00:10:32]. The timing playbook has also flipped. Mark Ryan says firms used to sub 70%, 40% and 10% across years and then self-perform in year four 'and get away with that,' which Ryan says no longer works because compliance now runs per contract year and, on IDIQs, per task order. Where FAR and SBA texts conflict, NSBGCA's DCAA speaker Amanda Reed answers simply: follow the contract.

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most common failure is leakage below the first tier. PilieroMazza's worked example has a prime performing 40% and a similarly situated sub performing 20%, but that sub farms out 15%, leaving the prime credited with only 45% and non-compliant [i9prjadeAyM @ 00:19:17]. Mark Ryan describes the same mechanic from the other direction: on a $100K 8(a) IT contract, $20K subbed to another 8(a) still counts toward the $50K, but any further subbing is clawed back [ne7XpEiLNKE @ 00:03:07]. Watson's rule of thumb is blunt: work by anyone other than the prime's employees or first-tier similarly situated employees counts against the prime [28K_7987r8w @ 00:09:10]. Vet GovCon Blueprint names three traps from running an SDVOSB prime: pass-through arrangements, mixed status where the sub's status does not match the set-aside, and silent drift over time, summed up as 'Certifications lapse' [go1eoNNgFRM @ 00:04:20]. Their fix is mechanical, tracking dollars to each sub monthly, and PilieroMazza sets the floor at monthly tracking and no less than quarterly. Back-loading is dead as a recovery plan: PilieroMazza calls 'we'll make it up' over the remaining years the most common misconception, because compliance is measured per base or option period and shortfalls cannot be recovered later.

The economics check starts with the math, and the math is easy to get wrong. PilieroMazza's worked example of $1M per month with $100K in materials produces a $450K self-performance requirement [i9prjadeAyM @ 00:32:49], and Vet GovCon Blueprint shows that on a $100K services contract, paying $70K to one non-similarly-situated sub breaks the rule. GovPrep's own example illustrates the danger of trusting a speaker's arithmetic: the GovPrep speaker says a '$100,000 contract' requires '$500,000,' which does not reconcile with the stated 50% services rule [bg9NY9VUfsE @ 00:04:23]. Getting it wrong is expensive. Mark Ryan reports that COs are now required to give a negative CPARS for missing the requirement [ne7XpEiLNKE @ 00:05:33], PilieroMazza lists suspension, debarment and fines and reports DOJ investigations rising, and Amanda Reed of DCAA, speaking at NSBGCA, adds withheld payments, treble damages under the False Claims Act, termination for default, and suspension or debarment [ka1Q_JhjM8w @ 00:19:40]. Watson's hedge against False Claims and pass-through scrutiny is to have subs certify compliance with each invoice, though Watson concedes no case law supports it. Federal-funds enforcement reach shows in Court Files' report of 47 ghost-student cases across 27 of the FBI's 55 field offices, though Scamverge stresses these are charges, not convictions.

Status and paperwork traps sink primes who trust the wrong document. PilieroMazza says primes may rely on a sub's SAM or written representations as of the subcontract offer date, but HUBZone status requires confirming SBA certification and SDVOSB self-certification ended in January 2023 [i9prjadeAyM @ 00:24:39]; the firm's defensive clause requires prompt notice of status changes plus indemnification. On affiliation, Watson flags 70% or more of revenue from one company in the prior year as economic dependence and treats an incumbent sub as a red flag under the ostensible subcontractor rule, while stressing 'there is no bright line rule every case is fact specific' and that 'affiliation is a rebuttable presumption' [k1ZkyITmwWM @ 00:04:50]; Watson's firm won Argus & Black after OHA held that mechanically applying economic dependence to a startup was wrong. Flow-downs are the third trap. Devine Hewitt warns 'Most primes flow everything down,' including clauses that do not apply to the sub, and tells subs to reject blanket comply-with-everything language [yp5LO51vPi8 @ 00:18:25]. Chase K. of Capital Edge adds that naming a sub during negotiations does not satisfy 52.244-2, and that consent must be written consent from the CO because verbal consent does not count [36eRQkU2X_I @ 00:13:16].

callout.title: Four checks before the subcontract dollars move
callout.body: Each check maps to a failure a practitioner watched happen or warned about directly; clear all four before signing a sub or submitting an invoice.
items: Confirm the staff and infrastructure to self-perform exist before bidding, or be ready to withdraw the bid [PilieroMazza PLLC — i9prjadeAyM @ 00:04:28].

Verify every similarly situated sub is first tier, holds the same program status, and is small under the NAICS assigned to the subcontract, not the prime's NAICS [Theodore Watson — 28K_7987r8w @ 00:04:26].

chapters.question_prompt: Which parts of the FAR actually matter to a small contractor, and how is the FAR overhaul changing them?
chapters.title: Navigating the FAR and Contract Administration
chapters.subtitle: FAR structure and the parts that matter, Part 1 authority and unauthorized commitments, Part 4 registration data and CAGE updates, Part 34 scope, schedule and cost, Part 52 clauses, Part 47 transportation and FOB terms, Part 33 protests vs. claims, and the Revolutionary FAR Overhaul
chapters.executive_summary: Practitioners from PCI, GovSuccess, Contract Warrior, FedAccess, Neybor and GovCon Empire converge on one operating rule: only the contracting officer binds the government, and the clauses physically in your contract govern your money. Tim Sullivan and Christopher Williams both treat CORs as having zero contracting authority, and Williams describes a contractor filing a roughly $38k REA after a COR-directed ductwork move. Street mechanics center on Ctrl-F for '52.2', checking clause dates, flagging the 30-day change notice, the 60-day/75% limitation-of-cost warning, and $100,000 claim certification. FAR overhaul operators report about 25% of the text moved to companion guides and Part 12 awards in roughly 45 days versus 5+ months under Part 15. They split on how to read clause numbers, how many pages the FAR runs, and whether to read it at all.

sections.heading: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: The hardest consensus in this chapter is about who can spend the government's money. GovSuccess opens FAR Part 1 with a customer asking for extra work and says the first question is authority, not enthusiasm: contracting officers bind the government only within delegated authority, while a COR works under a written designation and cannot change price, quantity, delivery or terms [x7xmTiXnwQ4 @ 00:00:17]. Tim Sullivan of PCI, who logged two years as a contracting officer and decades as a contractor lawyer, hammers the same line in plain terms: CORs have no contracting authority, so loop every scope question back to the CO, in writing [Gisvrg813kY @ 01:12:28]. Christopher Williams, a KO for 17 years, puts teeth on it from the construction side: a COR carries no warrant and cannot alter the scope of work [pktnZU4AWIE @ 00:04:31]. Sky and Michelle, former Air Force procurement litigators, add why this bites so often: constructive changes frequently happen orally in meetings, and the changes clause expects the contractor to notify the CO, typically within 30 days, though they tell operators to read the actual clause [h1yszOmFw3w @ 00:14:08]. GovSuccess adds that job titles, relationships and urgency never create authority, and that ratification is a conditional process, not a dependable business plan.

The second point of agreement: the clauses inside your own contract are what you actually live under, and they carry real legal weight. Sullivan reports that courts hold the FAR has the force and effect of law, and that a FAR violation that hurt a protester means the solicitation is probably going down [Gisvrg813kY @ 00:13:10]. David Gallagher of Kutak Rock, with 20-plus years in the field, maps the stack: the FAR sits in 48 CFR Chapter 1, and agency supplements such as DFARS and HSAR usually add to it and occasionally displace it, with data rights and country of origin as the examples [UV6zJLRHfHw @ 00:09:38]. FedAccess frames the operator version bluntly: the FAR runs about 2,000 pages, so don't read it, read your clauses, because invoicing, progress payments and fast payment are set by your contract rather than by generic FAR searching [T_cRpZF2IUo @ 00:00:00]. ASI Education lands in the same place from a study angle, noting Part 52 is the only part addressed to the contractor and the longest, and recommending one clause a day [MTy_zJd0RsY @ 00:02:41]. Gallagher counts more than 600 clauses and splits them into instructional, certification, prohibition and requirement buckets, with requirement-clause noncompliance meaning breach or default.

The third consensus covers the FAR overhaul: buying is getting faster, but the text you read online may not be the text your agency implemented. Sullivan traces the April executive order, Restoring Common Sense to Federal Procurement, which kept only content required by law or essential to sound procurement, and reports about 25% of the FAR moved to companion guides that cannot support protests [Gisvrg813kY @ 00:18:42]. Derrick Green, an ex-CO at DoD, DHS, FEMA, VA and Houston, tells vendors to have pricing, staffing, insurance, references and an operational story ready because awards may now arrive in days, not months [k1EsNHPfqXY @ 00:09:13]. GovSuccess runs the counterweight across multiple episodes: an overhaul model is not automatically the text your agency implemented [z7tDxORX_pQ @ 00:01:42], and codified and overhaul section numbers differ, so the operator has to verify which version actually applies [LgX6N2c9-S4 @ 00:00:33]. Fed Gov Today's guest Matthew Rose of Snowflake describes the culture shift behind it: more commercial technology buying, Part 10 market research, and agencies paying for outcomes rather than level of effort. Green's line on the tempo is that faster does not mean reckless, it just means smarter.

sections.heading: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: The clause-reading workflow starts with a keyword hunt. Gallagher's tactic is to Ctrl-F the solicitation for '52.2' to surface every FAR clause, then repeat for the supplement prefixes: DFARS clauses start with 252, GSA with 552 and VA with 852 [UV6zJLRHfHw @ 00:29:28]. Clauses show up in full text or by reference in Sections H, I and K, and the date matters: 52.243-1 dated April 1984 versus August 1987 is unchanged after 37 years, but Buy American versions from February 2009 and October 2022 differ materially. An undated clause most likely means the version in effect at signing, and Gallagher calls the idea of a self-refreshing clause wrong, just as there is no such thing as a self-deleting flow-down [UV6zJLRHfHw @ 00:38:30]. FedAccess's shortcut for the unfamiliar ones is to Google the clause together with its date [T_cRpZF2IUo @ 00:03:04]. Sullivan adds a tracing step: every clause says 'as prescribed by' a section, so trace each clause back to its prescription, and use the 52.3 matrix, which codes clauses R, A or O [Gisvrg813kY @ 00:57:25]. On fill-ins, Gallagher's rule is short: blank means blank, and the government cannot fill in a 52.244-2 blank six months later.

Post-award money runs on hard clocks. Sky and Michelle's numbers: notify the CO of a change typically within 30 days, recover the cost of the change plus reasonable profit, and remember commercial contracts allow no constructive change [h1yszOmFw3w @ 00:14:08]. Williams ties the same 30-day notice to the changes clause and warns that late claims are scraping the pan, because costs still have to be allowable, allocable and reasonable [pktnZU4AWIE @ 00:05:12]. Sullivan's rule while a dispute runs is to keep performing as directed and file a claim in parallel; the example is quoting $2M while the agency offers $1M [Gisvrg813kY @ 00:39:41]. The KW partners then stack the claim math: claims over $100,000 must be certified and start the disputes process, the limit is six years, CDA interest runs on claims, and REA preparation costs are recoverable but REAs earn no CDA interest [h1yszOmFw3w @ 01:01:54]. Their other clocks include a limitation-of-cost notice within 60 days of reaching 75%, a termination-for-convenience settlement proposal within one year with an inventory schedule inside 120 days, a 10-day cure notice for some default grounds, and 90 days to the board or a year to the Court of Federal Claims to appeal a default.

On the front end, Neybor Consulting lays out the Part 12 economics: more than 60% of federal buys use commercial authority, FAR 2.0 raises the threshold to $7.5M or $15M in emergencies, and a Part 12 award takes about 45 days versus 5-plus months under Part 15 [TFl20T0yyig @ 00:02:10]. The timeline Neybor teaches is a synopsis of about 15 days, evaluation in 1 to 4 weeks and award in 30 to 60 days, with the contractor signing block 30 and the CO signing block 31; firm-fixed-price is the default, so price accordingly, and cost-type is prohibited [TFl20T0yyig @ 00:15:50]. FedAccess flags that SCA and Davis-Bacon wage determinations drive pricing and that 52.219-14 limitations on subcontracting matters for middleman strategies. GovSuccess pushes delivery math: compare FOB origin and destination quotes on a total-delivered-cost basis covering freight, packaging, appointments and unloading, because the lowest unit price may not produce the lowest supported delivery cost [QvsXldnQyAg @ 00:02:31]. Registration hygiene closes the loop. Federal Processing Registry says to update a CAGE record within 30 days of an address, ownership or structure change; DLA review takes 3 to 7 business days, and past 10 days you call the DLA Customer Interaction Center [ifMU9O8Ydmg @ 00:01:23].

callout.title: Moves the veterans actually run
callout.body: Small habits from former contracting officers and procurement litigators that protect bid money, flow-down exposure and pricing.
items: Never wait until the last minute: an electronic proposal sent before 5:00 the prior day and delayed by government fault must be accepted, otherwise late is late, and even when you win, ask for a debriefing [Public Contracting Institute (PCI) — Gisvrg813kY @ 00:26:41].
Treat local clauses as the dangerous ones: they skip public comment, which is why Sullivan calls them doozies [Public Contracting Institute (PCI) — Gisvrg813kY @ 01:01:45].
Don't flow down all of 52.2 to subs; the mandatory lists live in 52.244-6 and 52.212-5(e), and 244-7000 tells primes to limit flow-downs [Public Contracting Institute (PCI) — UV6zJLRHfHw @ 00:56:54].
Under TINA, exempt under $2M, you must disclose a cheaper vendor you know about when pricing [How To Sell To & Win Federal Government Contracts — h1yszOmFw3w @ 00:39:13].

sop_steps.title: Build the authority sheet
sop_steps.action: List the contracting officer, the designated technical representative, your authorized company signer and your internal escalation owner, and keep the award, modifications and delegations accessible.
sop_steps.detail: Drill staff on where to route scope requests so the team responds promptly without making commitments based on assumptions [Win Government Contracts with GovSuccess — x7xmTiXnwQ4 @ 00:01:24].

sop_steps.title: Map every clause and its date
sop_steps.action: Ctrl-F '52.2' and the supplement prefixes, note full-text versus by-reference clauses in Sections H, I and K, and record each clause date.
sop_steps.detail: Treat an undated clause as the version at signing, never assume self-refresh or self-deleting, and remember blank means blank [Public Contracting Institute (PCI) — UV6zJLRHfHw @ 00:29:28].

sop_steps.title: Route and document every change
sop_steps.action: When a COR or field rep directs work outside scope, stop and get the KO's confirmation before performing.
sop_steps.detail: Send the 30-day changes-clause notice and keep costs allowable, allocable and reasonable, because late claims are scraping the pan [Contract Warrior — pktnZU4AWIE @ 00:06:55].

sop_steps.title: Split protest files from claim files
sop_steps.action: Open a protest file (action, interest, forum, filing rules) separate from a claim file (contractual basis, relief, certification).
sop_steps.detail: Never import protest deadlines into a claim or confuse the submission period with the appeal period, and keep evidence of delivery and receipt [Win Government Contracts with GovSuccess — -smvR-8_v1M @ 00:00:55].

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The first split is how deep to go into the regulation itself. FedAccess says the FAR runs 2,000 pages and flatly tells operators not to read it. Instead, read the clauses in your own solicitation, then Google each clause with its date [T_cRpZF2IUo @ 00:00:00]. ASI Education runs the opposite drill: memorize all 53 parts with the "Colt 45" mnemonic, read Part 52 one clause a day, and master Parts 15 and 13 [MTy_zJd0RsY @ 00:01:47]. ASI also anchors its read on 1.102(d): "if it's not prohibited it's okay." Even the clause numbering gets read two ways. FedAccess parses 52.219-14 as subpart 2, section 219, and flags it as the limitations-on-subcontracting clause that matters for middleman strategies [T_cRpZF2IUo @ 00:02:44]. David Gallagher of Kutak Rock reads the digits after 52.2 as the FAR part that prescribes the clause, and says the "numerology nomenclature" alone tells you where a clause lives and why [UV6zJLRHfHw @ 00:30:26]. Gallagher adds that supplements carry their own prefixes: DFARS 252, GSA 552 and VA 852. The page count splits too, with ASI Education saying 1,000 plus pages and FedAccess saying 2,000. Pick one reading system, but trace every clause back to its prescription and date before you price.

The FAR overhaul splits the room between operators sprinting for speed and operators slowing down to verify the text. Derrick Green "Theo," an ex-CO at DoD, DHS, FEMA, VA and Houston, says to stop wasting six months pretending 200 vendors exist. Have pricing, staffing, insurance, references and an operational story ready, because you may get "days, not months" [k1EsNHPfqXY @ 00:09:13]. Neybor Consulting pushes the same tempo through Part 12. More than 60 percent of federal buys use commercial authority, FAR 2.0 raises the threshold to $7.5M or $15M in emergencies, and a Part 12 award lands in about 45 days versus 5+ months under Part 15 [TFl20T0yyig @ 00:02:10]. GovSuccess runs the counter-playbook. Its Part 34 breakdown warns that an overhaul model is not automatically the text your agency implemented. Its Part 47 breakdown adds that FAC 2026-01, effective March 13, 2026, still has to be checked against deviations [z7tDxORX_pQ @ 00:01:42]. Fed Gov Today guest Matthew Rose of Snowflake reports a pricing split as well: buyers are moving from paying for level of effort to paying for outcomes, yet utility-based pricing is still "not the norm" [MM4DJrI2Od0 @ 00:02:16]. Neybor's hedge is blunt: expect FFP and price accordingly.

When a fight starts, practitioners split on which lever to pull. Tim Sullivan says a FAR violation that impacted the protester means the solicitation is "probably going down." Yet in one sole-source dispute, Sullivan skipped the protest and wrote to the competition advocate instead [Gisvrg813kY @ 00:23:38]. Sullivan also warns that the overhaul moved about 25 percent of the FAR into companion guides, and that material cannot support protests. On performance disputes, Sullivan's playbook is to keep performing as directed and file a claim in parallel, using the case where you quote $2M and the agency offers $1M [Gisvrg813kY @ 00:39:41]. Sky and Michelle, former Air Force procurement litigators, agree that the disputes clause demands continued performance. They add that a breach exists only for a cardinal change, so get counsel before stopping, and that commercial contracts allow no constructive change at all [h1yszOmFw3w @ 00:12:48]. GovSuccess refuses to blend the two paths. A protest file tracks action, interest, forum and filing rules. A claim file tracks contractual basis, relief and certification. A clarification request, debriefing, REA and claim are not interchangeable [-smvR-8_v1M @ 00:00:55]. Gallagher adds a subcontract wrinkle: the majority view keeps the Christian doctrine off subcontracts, and Chevron changes likely limit it further.

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most expensive trap reported firsthand is working off a COR's say-so. Christopher Williams of Contract Warrior, a KO for 17 years, walks through a construction job where the COR ordered ductwork offset 6 feet north. Three weeks later, the contractor filed an REA of about $38k [pktnZU4AWIE @ 00:04:13]. The COR had no warrant and could not alter the scope of work. The 30-day notice under the changes clause was blown, and a late claim at that point is "scraping the pan." Williams adds that costs still have to be allowable, allocable and reasonable, and that the COR could end up paying [pktnZU4AWIE @ 00:06:37]. Tim Sullivan hits the same wall from the lawyer side: a COR has no contracting authority, so loop scope questions back to the CO, in writing [Gisvrg813kY @ 01:12:28]. GovSuccess closes the escape hatch contractors bank on. Ratification is a separate process with conditions, and it is not a dependable business plan for work started without proper authorization. Job titles, relationships and urgency do not establish authority [x7xmTiXnwQ4 @ 00:00:50]. Sky and Michelle note that constructive changes often happen orally in meetings, which is exactly where unwritten direction gets lost.

The money leaks come from pricing assumptions, not just authority. FedAccess reports a firm that lost money on Service Contract Act paid vacation. The channel also warns that the government can terminate for convenience and has done so shortly after award [T_cRpZF2IUo @ 00:05:54]. Tim Sullivan, who says there is no three-offeror rule, describes a client rated in the '50s that spent "150 grand" chasing an award; the case settled. Agencies can also award on initial proposals, so holding back for best-and-finals is a gamble [Gisvrg813kY @ 00:30:24]. Sullivan's other losses are procedural. A bid that took exception to the default clause was rejected as nonresponsive. Late is late, unless an electronic submission sent before 5:00 the prior day was delayed by the government's fault. GovSuccess flags a hidden cost in schedules: a sensor program had a June test slot with no priced retest, and money spent is not the same thing as completed technical work [z7tDxORX_pQ @ 00:02:18]. On supply deals, the same channel warns that the lowest unit price may not produce the lowest supported delivery cost. Compare FOB origin and destination quotes on freight, packaging, appointments and unloading [QvsXldnQyAg @ 00:02:49].

The quietest failures are missed clocks and dirty records. Sky and Michelle lay out the deadlines that sink contractors: settlement proposals within 1 year of a termination for convenience, and inventory schedules within 120 days. A default can be appealed within 90 days to the board or within a year to the Court of Federal Claims, and default records damage you in SAM [h1yszOmFw3w @ 00:27:49]. Claims over $100,000 must be certified, and the claim window runs 6 years. REA preparation costs are recoverable, but REAs earn no CDA interest [h1yszOmFw3w @ 01:03:30]. GovSuccess warns operators not to import protest deadlines into a claim, and not to confuse the submission period with the appeal period. On registration, Federal Processing Registry says to update your CAGE code within 30 days of an address, ownership or structure change. DLA review takes 3 to 7 business days, and past 10 days you call the DLA Customer Interaction Center. "Entity not found" means you need to update IRS data [ifMU9O8Ydmg @ 00:01:23]. David Gallagher adds a drafting trap: if the 52.244-2 blank is left empty, the government cannot fill it in 6 months later, because "blank means blank" [UV6zJLRHfHw @ 00:44:39]. Unmarked data submissions, per Sky and Michelle, put your rights at risk.

callout.body: Before any extra work starts, before any bid goes out, and before any dispute gets a label, clear these four gates drawn from losses the practitioners saw firsthand.
items: No scope change moves until the KO confirms it; a COR has no warrant and cannot alter the scope of work [Contract Warrior — pktnZU4AWIE @ 00:06:55].

chapters.question_prompt: How do I find, source, quote and batch-bid DLA parts solicitations on DIBBS?
chapters.title: Brokering DLA Parts Through DIBBS
chapters.subtitle: Finding RFQs by FSC, NSN and due date, extracting key RFQ data, finding the right supplier, urgent-need and no-bid lists, AMSC manufacturing RFQs, live solicitation review and bidding, batch quote files and the DLA BUS, and Intertek/SAI tools
chapters.executive_summary: DLA brokers on DIBBS agree the game is volume inside a narrow lane: register on SAM and DIBBS, pick three to five FSCs, screen each RFQ for approved-source restrictions, and quote every day, because roughly 99% of awards go to the cheapest bid and bid count tracks award count. Street mechanics are precise: read solicitations only to page 10, anchor price to procurement history, target 10 to 15% margin, take Net 30 since the government pays in 23 to 25 days, and call suppliers instead of emailing. Tooling splits the field, from FedOpp's browser-built batch files to DVN's DLA BUS catalog uploads and Gov Scraper at $100 a month. Practitioners clash over chasing RFQs older than 60 days, whether batch bidding needs thousands of NSNs, and how fast a bidding catalog can realistically be built.

key_metrics.context: Ki Hendris of National Material Supply reports DLA posts 2,000 to 3,000 solicitations a day and often cancels and reissues them.

sections.heading: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every practitioner opens at the same front door: register on SAM to pull a UEI and CAGE code, then complete a separate DIBBS registration before a single quote goes in [wxZNfwOuung @ 00:02:38]. The prize behind that paperwork is enormous and tilted toward small shops. Ki Hendris of National Material Supply puts last year's DLA spend at $51.4 billion, with about 80% of awards going to small businesses [jjX9klCZFKI @ 00:10:46]. Tristan Thomas of Mend Sourcing and Gov Scraper counts $52.6 billion in 2024 obligations and $47 billion in revenue, with over 40% flowing to small business against a 5% SDVOSB goal [v7nJCLRc0uo @ 00:12:06]. DVN frames the daily firehose: about 10,000 awards a day, more than 100,000 open solicitations, 5 to 8 million NSNs, and roughly $50 billion a year [MyfmHjDF9HI @ 00:12:48]. The percentages differ by speaker, but the direction is identical: this is a small-business market moving thousands of buys every day, and the operators who win are the ones who treat it as a daily volume game rather than a lottery ticket. None of these operators sells it as fast money; the work is registration, a narrow lane, and relentless quoting.

The second agreement is the lane, and the lane is the Federal Supply Class. Thomas says about 95% of searches run by the four-digit FSC, and filtering 5306, 5305 and 5310 to small business and SDVOSB set-asides returned 876 RFQs in a single pull [v7nJCLRc0uo @ 00:18:41]. myContractScout tells newcomers to start with three to five FSCs, aim for a first $100,000, and stay disciplined about scope: don't go try to sell tires on day one [SeWe_WAhyVg @ 00:08:07]. The third agreement is that approved-source restrictions decide whether a broker can even play the buy. Tris10 tells beginners to look for items whose PID is blank with no approved sources, which any supplier can fill, and to pair those with local manufacturers [JE_OOJ3NAVk @ 00:09:49]. FedOpp warns flatly that the codes limiting a buy to approved sources can knock you out, and puts an AMSC filter directly on its bid-board search for exactly that reason [bTlxn6BVHJ0 @ 00:02:02]. The operator logic stacks cleanly: keep a short FSC list, screen every RFQ for who is allowed to supply the part, and spend sourcing hours only where the door is open or where a distributor can reach the named manufacturer.

The final consensus is that awards follow volume, price, and voice. Tris10 states there is a direct correlation between the amount of bids you put into the system and the amount of awards you win, and pushes operators to keep quoting even when they suspect they are priced out [v4ulUMKE5xA @ 00:15:55]. Humam Finding Sam estimates about 99% of awards go to the cheapest bid, which makes the cheapest landed cost the entire contest [wxZNfwOuung @ 00:06:24]. Thomas ranks DLA's priorities in order: price first, then delivery time, then credibility through the SPRS score [v7nJCLRc0uo @ 00:30:17]. On the supplier side the agreement is just as firm. Tris10 says phone beats email and in person beats phone, because it is much harder for someone to say no to you over the phone than it is via email [JE_OOJ3NAVk @ 00:11:07]. That makes the daily rhythm obvious for a broker: a short FSC list, aggressive price-first quoting every day, delivery treated as a secondary lever, and suppliers worked by voice instead of by inbox. Price is the contest, and volume is how an operator gets enough at-bats to win it.

sections.heading: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Execution starts with the pull. On raw DIBBS, myContractScout runs FSC 6510, gets 452 records, and copies the whole list into Google Sheets to work it outside the portal [SeWe_WAhyVg @ 00:06:21]. FedOpp's morning routine is tighter: filter Parts to Quote down to open RFQs only, then sort by last award unit price before building any quote [bTs2wy13K1c @ 00:03:21]. Reading the solicitation is where most hours disappear, and Thomas cuts it hard. They read only through page 10 of a 24-page RFQ, up to the asterisks, and extract the solicitation number, PR number, procurement history, NSN, CMMC level, approved sources, CLIN quantity, delivery days, FOB terms, and ASTM packaging; their worked example carried 831 units at 108 delivery days with FOB origin, meaning the government pays shipping [v7nJCLRc0uo @ 00:23:27]. Tris10 treats procurement history as the price compass. One shear bolt history showed 1,966 pieces at $556 in 2022 and 46 pieces at $49.90 in 2021, which gives a broker the price band before calling a single supplier [Z9MLGFqFXtM @ 00:02:17]. The extraction sheet becomes the template for every vendor request, so the same dozen fields get captured the same way on every RFQ.

Pricing is built backward from the last award, not forward from a supplier list. Humam Finding Sam pulls past awards of $33 on February 25, 2026, $35 on January 28, and $27 on August 4, 2025, so they enter the vendor request already knowing what the item should cost [wxZNfwOuung @ 00:06:38]. DVN's live wiper-blade bid shows the markup math in plain dollars: a 10% markup came to about $2 per unit and $642 of total profit, with ASTM D3951 packaging and MIL-STD-129 labels priced in [MyfmHjDF9HI @ 00:31:22]. Thomas puts the sweet spot at 10 to 15% margin, warns that asking 20 to 30% gets you underbid, and walks a worked build: 250 units at $185 for $46,250, plus a $350 packaging minimum, plus a 250 DCMA inspection line, plus $7,035 of margin, all divided by 250 for the unit bid [v7nJCLRc0uo @ 00:38:03]. Terms move cash too. Tris10 picks Net 30 over a 10-day term because the shorter term is a 2% haircut that turns $100,000 into $98,000, and the government pays within 23 to 25 days on average anyway [v4ulUMKE5xA @ 00:05:57]. The pattern across all four is identical: anchor on history, stack every landed cost, add a thin margin, and protect it through payment terms.

The bid form is where volume is won or lost. Tris10's rule on the DIBBS web quote is to keep filling until no section is still yellow [v4ulUMKE5xA @ 00:02:32]. Hendris lays out the three quoting methods: the web form at about two pages and time-consuming, EDI through a value-added network that is antiquated, expensive, and not recommended for small businesses, and batch quoting as a one-click upload locked to active vendors [jjX9klCZFKI @ 00:11:21]. Batch is where the serious distributors live, and the tooling filters dead lines before they waste an upload. DVN's DLA BUS demo pushed 20 solicitations through and returned 11 green passes and 9 red failures that were already awarded, cancelled, or closed [YlwuuaCoHzQ @ 00:12:25]. FedOpp's batch builder runs a Check Line pass that flags every error in red with a running count of items left to fix, covering item description code, quality, trade and Buy American answers, packaging, and manufacturer or dealer fields [iTxJkLPYuqc @ 00:02:56]. The street logic is simple: a web form handles a few quotes a day, but an operator chasing real volume moves the prep into spreadsheets or a catalog, validates every line against DLA's format, and uploads the whole stack at once instead of retyping CAGE codes and prices one solicitation at a time.

callout.title: Edges the Volume Bidders Actually Use
callout.body: Four moves the practitioners use to quote faster, source cleaner, and stay in the running on more buys.
items: Map every NSN to the manufacturer part number before you call, because suppliers often have no idea what an NSN is; Tris10 uses the nsn-now public search to do it [Tris10 @ MeND — JE_OOJ3NAVk @ 00:04:05].
Quote your real lead time instead of the requested one: Thomas won with 300 days against 25 requested, because DLA ranks price ahead of delivery [Secureframe — v7nJCLRc0uo @ 00:30:17].
Build a manufacturing view by adding a filter where Approved Sources is null and hitting apply, so only RFQs open to small manufacturers remain [Loocey DLA & GovCon — LzmJyrGyMBw @ 00:00:34].
You do not need thousands of NSNs to batch bid: every NSN you bid, won or lost, joins your catalog, per Hendris [The DLA Vendor Network (DVN) — jjX9klCZFKI @ 00:20:13].

sop_steps.title: Lock the FSC lane on the bid board
sop_steps.action: Filter open DLA RFQs to your handful of FSCs, then layer the set-aside filter.
sop_steps.detail: FedOpp calls the FSC filter the fastest one because most shops quote a handful of classes, and pairs it with set-aside filters for small business, HUBZone and SDVOSB [FedOpp — bTlxn6BVHJ0 @ 00:01:38].

sop_steps.title: Extract the approved manufacturer and part number
sop_steps.action: Pull the named approved manufacturer and its part number from the RFQ before sourcing.
sop_steps.detail: Tris10 pulls the single approved manufacturer, SPS Technologies, and its part number, noting they can only go to SPS Technologies or find a company that can supply the part from SPS Technologies [Tris10 @ MeND — Z9MLGFqFXtM @ 00:03:37].

sop_steps.title: Send an all-inclusive vendor request
sop_steps.action: Email the supplier the NSN, part number, drawings and delivery date, then follow up by phone.
sop_steps.detail: Humam Finding Sam requests all-inclusive pricing including surcharges [Humam Finding Sam — wxZNfwOuung @ 00:08:06], and Tris10's template also asks for lead time, stock, certs, country of origin, cert fees and traceability [Tris10 @ MeND — JE_OOJ3NAVk @ 00:14:37].

sop_steps.title: Fill the dealer fields and submit, then revise
sop_steps.action: Enter the manufacturer's CAGE in the dealer field, submit, and circle back to revise while the RFQ is open.
sop_steps.detail: Tris10 enters the manufacturer's CAGE in the dealer field [Tris10 @ MeND — v4ulUMKE5xA @ 00:11:39], and DVN says to bid and bid often because you can always circle back and revise after submitting [The DLA Vendor Network (DVN) — MyfmHjDF9HI @ 00:35:56].

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split is over how old an RFQ can be before it becomes dead money. Tris10 @ MeND treats the return date loosely, using a no-bid as a placeholder and often bidding after expiration because DIBBS is more lenient than SAM, yet draws a hard line against touching anything older than 60 days and works the newest RFQs because a contracting officer just put them into the system [v4ulUMKE5xA @ 00:05:07]. Tristan Thomas of Mend Sourcing and Gov Scraper, speaking on Secureframe, lands in the same camp and calls the popular go-back-60-to-90-days advice false, arguing that stale RFQs are leftovers from DLA staff reassignment rather than proof that nobody bid, and sorts every search by newest issued [v7nJCLRc0uo @ 00:20:44]. The DLA Vendor Network runs a looser play in its live walkthrough: a wiper-blade solicitation whose September 28 deadline had passed was still open on October 4, and they quoted it anyway [MyfmHjDF9HI @ 00:25:44]. Their logic is bid and bid often, because a submitted bid can always be revised later [MyfmHjDF9HI @ 00:35:56]. The usable synthesis is that a passed return date alone does not kill a buy, but the age of the RFQ separates live demand from abandoned records.

Delivery promises and margin targets split the camp just as hard. On the wiper blades, The DLA Vendor Network faced a 284-day required delivery and bid 90 days, landing at $23.31 per unit after a 10% markup worth about $2 per unit and $642 in total profit [MyfmHjDF9HI @ 00:35:09]. Tristan Thomas argues the reverse on delivery: quote your real lead time, because they won with 300 days against 25 requested, and DLA ranks price first, then delivery, then credibility through the SPRS score [v7nJCLRc0uo @ 00:30:17]. Tris10 @ MeND backs the price-first ranking from a different angle, pricing 103 pieces at 120 delivery days and stating that the government does not have delivery days as the number one priority [v4ulUMKE5xA @ 00:09:28]. On margin, Tristan Thomas puts the sweet spot at 10 to 15%, warns that asking 20 to 30% gets you underbid, and reports that judging the profit dollar amount instead of the percentage brought more awards [v7nJCLRc0uo @ 00:38:03]. The DVN markup sits at the bottom of that band, so the live argument is whether to anchor on percentage or on dollars per award, and whether a short delivery promise is worth the risk of missing it.

Tooling and catalog strategy form the third fault line. Ki Hendris of National Material Supply, presenting for The DLA Vendor Network, flatly rejects the idea that you need thousands of NSNs to batch bid, because every NSN you bid, won or lost, joins your catalog [jjX9klCZFKI @ 00:20:13]. FedOpp takes the opposite design stance from the DVN catalog generator: the batch TXT is built line by line in the browser, checked against DLA's format rules, and uploaded by the user, and FedOpp never submits bids [iTxJkLPYuqc @ 00:00:04]. Even what to read before quoting is contested. Tris10 @ MeND tells bidders that flow-downs can be ignored until an award lands, arguing you do not need all the information at the beginning just to submit a bid [Z9MLGFqFXtM @ 00:05:42]. Tristan Thomas lists missing flowdowns among the five mistakes that sink vendors, next to not reading to the asterisks, trusting one quote, promising unachievable delivery and ignoring SPRS [v7nJCLRc0uo @ 00:45:05]. Both still read the front of the RFQ hard: Tris10 pulls solicitation and PR numbers, procurement history, NSN, approved manufacturer and CLIN quantities, and Tristan stops at page 10 of 24, so the real dispute is only whether flowdown review happens before the bid or after the award.

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most common bleed happens before a bid is ever typed. Tris10 @ MeND opens on suppliers who no-bid, never respond, or quote far above the eventual award, then admits they came to find out suppliers had no idea what an NSN number is, which is why each NSN now gets mapped to the supplier part number through the nsn-now public search [JE_OOJ3NAVk @ 00:03:52]. When a supplier still declines, they phone to ask why it was a no-bid instead of moving on blind [JE_OOJ3NAVk @ 00:15:51]. Humam Finding Sam flags the vendor-side margin killer: surcharges left out of a quote are either going to eat your profit margin or end the bid with a loss, so the request has to carry NSN, part number, drawings and delivery date and demand all-inclusive pricing [wxZNfwOuung @ 00:08:30]. Tristan Thomas closes the same loop from the other side: always follow an email with a call, including after a no-bid, because it is harder to say no to a person when you hear their voice [v7nJCLRc0uo @ 00:54:07]. The economic check is simple: no line goes into DIBBS on a single unverified number while lead time, certs, country of origin, cert fees and traceability are still unanswered.

DIBBS itself punishes sloppy operators. myContractScout warns that you cannot hit the Enter button to run a search, that a soldier-hand error means refresh and redo, and that the browser back button times the session out [SeWe_WAhyVg @ 00:05:23]. The DLA Vendor Network's demo upload of 20 solicitations passed only 11, with the other nine flagged red as already awarded, cancelled or closed, and the same session warns that DLA will tell you when you did not win but not when a buy was cancelled [YlwuuaCoHzQ @ 00:12:25]. Ki Hendris adds that DLA posts 2,000 to 3,000 solicitations a day and often cancels and reissues them, so a dead solicitation number is routine rather than a glitch [jjX9klCZFKI @ 00:32:59]. Manual entry, per the same DVN camp, compounds the damage, burning three to five minutes per bid with errors such as the wrong CAGE code or the wrong price. FedOpp's answer is a check-line pass that flags errors in red with a running count of items left to fix, and an exporter that only exports files that pass DLA's format rules [iTxJkLPYuqc @ 00:04:03]. The operator lesson: expect part of every batch to bounce, and recheck status before blaming your price.

Eligibility traps cost the most because they surface after the sourcing work is done. Tris10 @ MeND warns that parts from a non-qualifying country such as China or Afghanistan disqualify the quote, and states flatly, 'in our case, we only buy American' [v4ulUMKE5xA @ 00:12:48]. They also caution that a procurement-history line only shows that someone won the award; a cancellation or protest may have followed, so the past price is a guide rather than a lock [Z9MLGFqFXtM @ 00:02:03]. Ki Hendris answers a question about passing JCP tech data to an uncertified shop with 'No, it is not legal,' unless the manufacturer is also certified, a hard stop for brokers who want to hand C-folder drawings to an outside manufacturer [jjX9klCZFKI @ 00:34:01]. The DLA Vendor Network frames the volume side just as soberly: GovCon is not a sprint, no company has a 100% hit ratio, and the target of ten bids a day comes with traceability requests you should expect [MyfmHjDF9HI @ 00:40:33]. Run every quote past those three checks, origin, tech-data rights and documentation, before the price ever gets entered.

callout.title: Four Stops Before The Price Field
callout.body: Every DIBBS quote clears these four checks before a unit price gets entered, each drawn from a practitioner warning.
items: Origin check: confirm the part does not come from a non-qualifying country such as China or Afghanistan, because that disqualifies the quote [Tris10 @ MeND — v4ulUMKE5xA @ 00:12:48].
Tech-data check: never pass JCP technical data to a manufacturer that is not also certified, which Ki Hendris calls not legal [The DLA Vendor Network (DVN) — jjX9klCZFKI @ 00:34:01].
Source check: an approved-source CAGE in the PID is mandatory, though you may buy that part through a distributor [Tris10 @ MeND — JE_OOJ3NAVk @ 00:08:55].
Document check: always read the full solicitation on DIBBS before you quote [FedOpp — bTs2wy13K1c @ 00:02:49].

chapters.pull_quote: "There is a direct correlation between the amount of bids that you put into the system and the amount of awards that you win." Tris10 @ MeND (v4ulUMKE5xA @ 00:15:55).
action_checklist: Pick 3 to 5 FSCs in your lane, search DIBBS by Federal Supply Class, click Search instead of Enter, and log results in Google Sheets [myContractScout — SeWe_WAhyVg @ 00:08:07].
Build a saved 'MFG items' view filtered where Approved Sources is null, then confirm via the NSN pop-up and the DIBBS NSN page [Loocey DLA & GovCon — LzmJyrGyMBw @ 00:00:34].
Anchor your price on procurement history and past awards before calling vendors, since about 99% of awards go to the cheapest bid [Humam Finding Sam — wxZNfwOuung @ 00:06:24].
Send the RFQ email asking lead time, stock, certs, country of origin, cert fees and traceability, then follow up by phone [Tris10 @ MeND — JE_OOJ3NAVk @ 00:14:37].
Price at a 10 to 15% margin and judge the profit dollar amount rather than the percentage alone [Secureframe — v7nJCLRc0uo @ 00:38:03].
Clear every yellow field, choose Net 30, set quote validity at 30 to 45 days, and keep bid volume high [Tris10 @ MeND — v4ulUMKE5xA @ 00:02:32].
